In this year, 1966, syndicated crime is moving into Canada and this is not the time for us to abolish capital puhishment or to make things easier for these criminals. In recent years we have had evidence of bodies being buried in lime in Quebec. We are all familiar with the McLaughlan case in Vancouver and the fact 23033-198i
Criminal Code
that the two people who were to appear in court on a narcotics charge were murdered yesterday. Surely I need say nothing more, because it is obvious that syndicated crime is moving into Canada.
Should we make things easier for criminals, and should we make the laws weaker, encouraging contract killing? Many people have talked about the greatest deterrent in Canada to murder. What does the Mafia have as its deterrent to keep their gangs on the straight and narrow, to keep them from squealing or going soft on the job? I suggest they use the death penalty. Their members either stay in line or they are rubbed out. They are encased in cement and dropped to the bottom of a river, or put somewhere else where they are not seen again. Torture is not used and life imprisonment is not used,-and I am sure the crime syndicates could impose life imprisonments if they wanted to, but it would be a great nuisance. Their ultimate deterrent is the death penalty.
If that analogy is a good one, then society's greatest deterrent is the death penalty. We in this country have not reached the point that we do not need a deterrent. In recent years we have all observed that crime is becoming of major concern to the citizens of this country, as evidenced as recently as yesterday by the killings in Vancouver.
In view of all these facts, I have reached the conclusion that now is not the time to abolish capital punishment. Our society has not reached that point at which we can forget about this ultimate deterrent to murder. It is my duty in this house, not to protect my interests or necessarily the interests of my family, but to protect society. I certainly feel that if we in this house vote in favour of this resolution we will be doing a disservice to society and, in fact, weakening the moral fibre on which we depend so much to protect ourselves and the citizens of this country. Thank you, Mr. Speaker.

First, Mr. Speaker, I want the house to know that I do not intend to take up much of its time or to repeat all that has already been so well said concerning the abolition of the death penalty.
But I do wish to congratulate the Prime Minister (Mr. Pearson) and the party leaders who decided together that party lines would not enter into this discussion and that the vote would be free. And even if this has nothing to do with this debate, Mr. Speaker, I

March 24, 1966
Criminal Code
must say I am one of those who hope that party leaders will give their supporters more opportunities to deal with matters before us in a non-partisan manner and let them free to vote as they wish. This debate is proceeding with such serenity that, in my opinion, it is setting an edifying example.
In any case, I want to repeat what others have said earlier and what I have discovered many times myself, and that is the great surprise of a fairly large number of Canadians when they learned about the great ease with which the cabinet commuted sentences even in cases where no recommendation for mercy had been given or, indeed, in cases which involved crimes that had shocked the Canadian people. I think that such a situation has been going on for too long and it is time we put a stop to it.
As I said, Mr. Speaker, I listened with a great deal of attention to the comments that were made. Some very instructive things have been said, but I think that the speaker who impressed me most was the hon. member for Bow River (Mr. Woolliams), who made a dispassionate review of the situation. I realized that the hon. member is surely an excellent lawyer, and if I were ever charged with some crime and needed a good criminal lawyer, I think I would go to him.
There was no cheap display of emotion about his speech and I found his arguments most effective. He asked disturbing questions which I am sure will prompt the members of the house to try to find answers in all conscience.
I think this has been the debate for which members were best prepared, since I would say thousands of references and documents were quoted on the subject. We could, if necessary have agreed to forgo this debate, so that the question could be put forthwith because I feel that everyone has a rather good idea as to how he will vote. But as it is also our duty to throw light on these timely topics for the benefit of those whom we represent, this probably explains why each member wants to make his own comments.
Let us, therefore, assume our responsibilities in all conscience, in what I think is one of the most typical examples of the responsibility of the members of the house and after consulting the electorate and, up to a point, involving their conscience also.
I have studied all the letters and circulars which were sent me, and I have been struck by certain things. For instance, the letters from pressure groups or organized groups,

seemed to me in some cases prompted by certain leaders rather than by the natural desire of each individual to participate in the discussion.
[DOT] (7:10 p.m.)
I wonder if this has not precisely tended to blow up artificially the influence of those organized groups which favour the abolition of capital punishment.
I have been much more impressed by the large number of individual letters I received from my riding and from all over the country because I have had contacts all over the place. I told myself that those people who have gone to the trouble of writing me personally without outside pressures, without being urged by a well incorporated, organized and set up association probably expressed more authentic personal opinions than members of organized groups.
The personal testimonials I have received at home appear to be, to a very large extent favourable to the retention of capital punishment.
Mr. Speaker, there seems to be some sort of misunderstanding on this question. I heard members talk of those mediaeval methods, of that barbaric attitude which consists in killing people, but it should nevertheless be realized that progress has been made in that area. People are no longer hanged for peccadillos, or quartered on the public square; since 1961, capital murder has been defined.
Miscarriages of justice are almost impossible in the present circumstances and the people who are sentenced to the gallows have been found guilty of capital murder beyond all doubt, and on the basis of complete evidence.
I say, Mr. Speaker, that capital punishment must be retained in the present circumstances, because we are not ready for abolition.
I shall even add, at the risk of seeming cruel to those who are against the retention of the death penalty, that a great many of them give me the impression of dreaming. They tell us that in our enlightened era, the death penalty is no longer required and, at the same time, we hear in this house very urgent requests for the setting up of judicial inquiries on organized crime, which would indicate that our enlightened era is perhaps resorting to modern methods to kill with more refinement than in the past, to commit mass murders as in the past perhaps, in short,
March 24, 1966

to kill for purposes of personal ambition and profit unthought of in the past.
It has not been proved, therefore, that our civilization has reached the point where it can do without the death penalty, which surely gives food for thought to people bent on doing wrong.
There is another thing which impressed me a great deal, Mr. Speaker, and I think that members of the house should not minimize this intervention:	representatives of police
forces at every level have unanimously requested the retention of the death penalty.
We, legislators, must by all means support the law enforcement officers who are certainly justified in asking us to retain the death penalty in the present circumstances, because they realize too that we are not ready for the abolition of capital punishment.
The time will come perhaps when we can abolish the death penalty. But until I am given proof that subversive activities against the established order, sometimes with violence, can be controlled in our country, I shall not accept the abolition of capital punishment.
Mr. Speaker, as long as it has not been proven to me, that reasonable prevention of organized crime has been set up here, I shall refuse to vote for the abolition of the death penalty.
As long as it not proven to me, Mr. Speaker, that we are organized to provide efficient rehabilitation of criminals here, I shall refuse to vote for the abolition of the death penalty.
As long as it has not been proven to me that we have enough prisons, modern prisons, built according to 20th-century standards, to house all those prisoners or criminals and keep them busy at something constructive, I shall refuse to let the death penalty go.
As long as we do not have here enough experts, psychologists, sociologists and, finally, specialists in all fields who will help us precisely to rehabilitate those people we want to keep in jail until they die, I say it will be illusive to advocate the abolition of the death penalty.
No. I suggest, Mr. Speaker, that we must be realistic and say to ourselves that Canada took a great step forward in 1961, with the passage of legislation defining capital crime, capital murder.
I think we have gone through a stage. The next one will entail a reform of the penal code, in which there will be gradations in
Criminal Code
crimes; the granting of a little more leeway to judges; the organization of those jails where immates will be detained for life, according to modern standards; the training of those technicians and specialists who will look after rehabilitation; better preparation for ourselves to carry out prevention, of juvenile delinquency for instance; the continuation of the war on poverty, precisely to prevent the fostering of young bandits in the most deprived sectors of society.
All these things represent the stage we have to go through today before abolishing this crime deterrent called capital punishment and to act otherwise would be deceptive, I believe.
Mr. Speaker, I will now conclude my remarks. I will vote against the abolition of capital punishment, because in my opinion it is a hasty and deceptive legislation, and before passing any such legislation, we should rather undertake the reforms I men-tionned earlier, such as modern penitentiaries as well as the training of a qualified staff, and later a legislative reform to cope with this new situation.

Mr. Speaker, the resolution now before us has been discussed and carefully studied for many years in various countries.
It is not the first time the Canadian parliament deals with this question. I am sure this debate will give rise to an objective exchange of views that will enlighten the Canadian people on a matter that is more and more in the mind and conscience of Canadian parliamentarians.
It was difficult for the work group which considered this question for some weeks to bring forward in this house a better method of discussion that should not appeal to one's feelings and sentimentality and partisanship.
I hope this debate goes on in this serene atmosphere, free from all strain that might have distorted the findings of our study in some cases.
Each one of us, Mr. Speaker, will have to vote freely at the end of this debate on the timeliness of abolishing or retaining in our statutes the death penalty for criminals found guilty of homicides.
May I be permitted, Mr. Speaker, at the outset of my remarks, to embark on a digression and confess to the house that, in 1960, when we dealt with Bill C-6 intended to abolish the death penalty, I took part in the debate at that time. Then I made a study of

March 24, 1966
Criminal Code
the provisions of the Criminal Code respecting homicide and I made some reservations on the definition of this crime in our statutes.
The legislation on homicide, as defined in the act passed in 1960, does not satisfy me. At that time, I had suggested that capital punishment be suspended as long as the legislator would not succeed in establishing various degrees in murders.
I had also suggested that in the spirit of the legislation enacted in 1960, judicial error could cause irreparable wrong to some criminals.
But since that date, Mr. Speaker, after a review of the question and a closer study of the various reports of the royal commission appointed to investigate this important issue, I am not prepared, today, to uphold the argument for the abolition of capital punishment, as I had done in 1960.
However, what mostly influenced my opinion on this matter was obviously the amendment to the Criminal Code which was moved in this house, by way of Bill C-92, on May 23, 1961 by the former Minister of Justice, the hon. member for Kamloops (Mr. Fulton).
[DOT] (7:20 p.m.)
As a matter of fact, the intention of this Bill C-92 was to divide murder into two classes, namely capital murder and non-capital murder.
This bill was the long-awaited answer to a judicial need and contributed to eliminate, in several cases, judicial errors resulting from the appreciation of essential facts submitted to the consideration of judge and jury.
Since this bill was passed, the judge must impose capital punishment only in cases where a premeditated murder was committed, and even in such a case, this legislation gives the jury the authority to recommend that the convicted individual receive the clemency of the court.
Under that act, an accused sentenced to death for capital murder may de piano appeal to a higher court against his conviction.
As far as those who are convicted of noncapital murder, the legislation provides as punishment a sentence of life imprisonment. That, I think, was a great improvement over the former provisions of the Criminal Code.
Therefore, pursuant to that Act, persons accused of being indirect accomplices to a crime of homicide, either before or after the fact, can avoid the death penalty and be sentenced to life imprisonment.

Such was not the case before. Indeed, under the former provisions of the criminal code concerning homicide, persons indirectly implicated in such a crime were treated in the same way as the main murderer and were liable to the same penalty, that is the death penalty.
To my mind, the adoption of bill C-92 has had for effect to greatly reduce the risks of judicial errors.
In the history of our courts, It has never been proven beyond doubt, that miscarriages of justice had caused irreparable prejudice to some convicts.
Statistics show that one error out of
250,000	cases was committed in all the history of some countries' courts.
I say "irreparable prejudice" because under our present legal set up, the case of a person sentenced to death can be reviewed by judges of different courts of appeal, and as a last resort, the cabinet reviews carefully each case where the death penalty has been imposed.
Bill C-92 goes still further than the recommendations in the reports from the joint committee of the Senate and the House of Commons on capital punishment; it may be remembered that this committee sat for two years, namely in 1954 and 1955.
Members in this house will recall that this committee had recommended the retention of capital punishment and had also recommended that murder should not be qualified. However, Bill C-92 defined homicide as capital and non-capital murder, thereby going beyond the conclusions of the report presented by the joint committee of the Senate and the House of Commons.
What incites me also to change my mind as regards this question is the large increase of crimes in this country. I know that the abolitionists are going to say that this should not be considered as a determining factor as far as reaching an objective conclusion on this question is concerned.
Some of the members in this house will quote statistics so as to prove that, in some of the states in the United States and some other countries, the abolition of capital punishment did not contribute to any crime increase in those countries.
This is obviously a matter of interpretation. However, I should like to emphasize the fact that, in the province of Quebec, the incidence of homicide rose sharply during the last few years.
March 24, 1966

Unfortunately, I did not have time to make statistical research in the other provinces, but I should like to put in the record anyway the statistics I have for the province of Quebec.
A survey conducted on the number of homicides committed in Quebec from 1946 to 1965 provides us with the following figures: In 1946, 36 murders; in 1947, 32 murders; in 1948, 32 murders; in 1949, 29 murders; in 1950, 34 murders. Or an average of 32 murders a year for the five year period.
In 1951, 40 murders; in 1952, 42 murders; in 1953, 43 murders;, in 1954, 32 murders; in 1955, 36 murders. Or an average of 38 murders a year for the five-year period and an increase of 13 per cent over the five preceding years.
In 1956, 40 murders; in 1957, 37 murders; in 1958, 39 murders; in 1959, 44 murders; in 1960, 47 murders. Average for these five years: 41 murders, or an increase of 12 per cent over the five preceding years.
In 1961, 57 murders; in 1962, 45 murders; in 1963, 63 murders; in 1964, 54 murders; in 1965, 65 murders. Hence an average of 57 murders a year for the five year period 1961 to 1965 incl., and an increase of 28 per cent over the five preceding years.
I would like to point out, Mr. Speaker, that between 1961-65, a period during which the cabinet commuted death sentences, in addition to the statistics which I mentioned earlier, there was a considerable increase in the number of murders in the province of Quebec.
The following figures refer to our population:
In 1951, the province of Quebec had a population of 4,055,681.
In 1956, the population reached 4,628,378 inhabitants, an increase of 14.12 per cent of the five-year period; there was a 13 per cent increase in crime in the same period.
In 1961, the province of Quebec had a population of 5,259,211, an increase of 13.6 per cent for the five-year period, but during the same period, there was a 12 per cent increase in crimes.
On December 31, 1965, there was a population of 5,700,000 in Quebec, an increase of 11.4 per cent over the previous years, whilst the murder rate for the corresponding years showed an increase of 27 per cent.
In Quebec, since 1959, all death sentences have been commuted, and there was no execution; but at the same time, the rate of murders has doubled in our province in the last five years.
These statistics, Mr. Speaker, indicate an alarming and nearly desperate situation. All the members of this house understand that the province of Quebec has had a sad experience for the last few months in this respect.
We may recall the case of an ex-convict who had been sentenced to life imprisonment and who, having been released from the penitentiary after some years by the National Parole Board, a few months later cut the throats of four children.
Criminal Code
We all remember vividly the murder of two policemen which occurred in Montreal last year and in which the criminal, without batting an eye-lash, shot down two peace officers who were endeavouring to arrest the perpetrator of a bank robbery who had killed a person in the commission of his crime. All this shows that to my mind the time is ill-chosen to abolish the death penalty.
It will be said that it is not proven that the death penalty acts as a deterrent and can prevent a criminal from committing a crime. But what is not known is that there is no certainty either that the abolition of capital punishment would not lead to a greater number of crimes precisely because of the removal of this deterrent which is the death penalty.
It is impossible to assert that individuals who are not criminals now would not let themselves be led down the path of crime if we were to abolish capital punishment.
[DOT] (7:30 p.m.)
Mr. Speaker, from my experience in the practice of law, I believe that criminals give great importance to the penalties provided in the criminal code. How many times, in the practice of law, have we realized it.
Indeed, the bill before us provides no alternative, since the death penalty is to be replaced by life imprisonment; I submit that that is not a proper alternative.
Indeed, we do not have the assurance that the person sentenced to life imprisonment will remain there all his life since this resolution provides that the responsibility will lie with the governor in council to carry out his prerogatives concerning mercy.
Does life imprisonment mean a term of 10, 15, 20 years or more in this resolution? We do not know.
Experience has shown to date that in many cases, the parole board has released murderers sentenced to life imprisonment after a period of 10 to 12 years; and the same thing could happen when the governor in council chooses to exercise his prerogative of mercy.
We have been told, during this debate, that the abolition of the death penalty would show that our country has achieved a certain maturity, that our civilization has evolved; however, in a well-organized society, there are laws which ensure the preservation and protection of its members. Its rules and its laws must be adhered to by all individuals.

March 24, 1966
Criminal Code
The basic rules of society are the expression of what the latter prescribes and of the penalties it provides for the violation of its rules. Without penalties, rules have no effect; and the penalty must be proportional to the crime or offence committed.
It is by practising the virtue of justice that society can secure that balance, and it is by practising concurrently the virtue of charity with the virtue of justice that the individual will respect the life and property of his fellowmen.
The third part of the resolution deals with the prerogatives of mercy and pardon which may be exercised by the governor in council. I think it is placing a very heavy responsibility on the shoulders of members of the cabinet to provide that they will consider alone each case of mercy.
That is why I would suggest that a standing committee of the house made up of members of the various political parties-or, if preferable, the justice and legal affairs committee-be asked to consider on merit each case of mercy and that a report be subsequently transmitted to the governor in council so that he can decide on the appeal for mercy.
Of course, committee reports would not necessarily be binding on the cabinet since only the governor in council is entitled to reprieve a convict.
Nevertheless, the aim of this committee's studies would be to help the cabinet, in some cases, to reach decisions and it would still minimize the remote possibility of judicial errors that may occur from time to time.
During debates in the house, several members have already expressed their dislike of hanging, the mode of execution now in use. I agree with them on this matter and I believe this very primitive mode of execution should be replaced by the gas chamber or the electric chair.
In closing, I should like to say this. We live in a society ruled by laws; peace and order must prevail in it.
Each individual forming this society must understand that the law applies equally to everyone, that every law by its definition and concept calls for a sanction and penalty proportional to the crime and offence. And it is our duty and responsibility as parliamentarians to see that those laws and their penalties are applied, if we want our civilization to continue enjoying the prestige and reputation it now has.

Mr. Speaker, my intervention in this debate will be brief, because I do not want to repeat the arguments which were put forward so far. However, I want to show that my attitude concerning the matter of capital punishment, is serious and that I respect the opinions of others. My decision to vote against the motion before us, does not make me a propagandist of the retention, who is trying to convince the abolitionists and prove them they are completely wrong. On the contrary, I believe that, under the present circumstances, there is some good in the position of both groups and I even think it is easier to be an abolitionist in the face of the rapid social evolution of our civilized world, since abolitionists are considered as reformists and seem to be more modern than we are.
Mr. Speaker, since I am basically in favour of the retention of capital punishment, I must admit that all the arguments advanced so far have not yet convinced me of the necessity for completely abolishing from our law this punishment, that some consider as barbaric. I am ready to admit that it is desirable to use it in a more and more limited way, as we improve our penal system, but, it is hard for me to think that I shall become convinced of the necessity of its total abolishment. Besides, it is not the punishment itself which concerns me most, but rather the fact that this punishment remains a usable instrument hanging over the heads of the criminals, as the spear of Damocles.
Therefore, the resolution in its present form, gives me no alternative, except if it is amended in order to maintain the death penalty for at least a certain number of crimes, among which the murder of police officers and prison guards on duty, as well as for some capital murders. It might be desirable that in this last instance, more leeway be made available to the judge, so that he may use clemency, replacing death penalty by life imprisonment when circumstances warrant.
Capital punishment is considered by many as a deterrent, some see it as a punishment or the repayment of a debt toward the society. Others consider it as barbaric, scandalous, as contrary to our principles of Christian charity. I considered all these points, I searched for an answer in statistics, the scriptures and literature published on this issue but I have always failed to convince myself that I should change my original opinion.
March 24, 1966

It is not only the question of playing with statistics, of setting forth a number of pros and cons, of appealing to our civilized spirit, but also there is another factor, which is one of personal feeling and what we feel deeply in our soul and conscience.
In regard to this issue, Mr. Speaker, we must ask ourselves whether we really want to protect society; whether we are not becoming more sympathetic to the criminal than to his victim or eventual victims. It is our responsibility to provide this additional protection to our policemen, to our law officers and to our prison guards. This is a very risky job, the danger is sometimes great and these people, who also have wives and children, risk their lives to protect society. Should we be selfish enough to deprive them from the maximum protection, even though certain groups or associations, in the name of civilization, term the death penalty as barbaric. Have you ever talked to a prison guard. Have you ever thought of gangland activities within and outside the walls of such institutions? Is there any difference, as far as a murderer is concerned, between one, two or three life sentences? He only has to say: "Put it on my bill" and he will be ready to start again the day after.
[DOT] (7:40 p.m.)
It is ridiculous to see what is being done and said in the name of liberty, human rights and civilization in this 20th century. One wonders who has more rights; the respectable, quiet and law-abiding citizen, the forces of law and order, who have the responsibility to pass and implement laws? I wonder, when I look at the activities of some of our fellow citizens. Even here in this house, Mr. Speaker, certain groups of members show more eagerness in defending criminal's, spies, in-corrigibles, than in defending the reputation and the integrity of the public servants; and they sometimes are prone to denounce police forces.
Another thing that strikes me is that many abolitionists are among those who are against our maximum security institutions. We saw it this week when a group of women called on us. They are against building fortresses to hold those who cannot be reformed, who cannot be saved-and there are some, believe me-but how is society going to protect itself? It is all very well to talk about rehabilitation, but it must not be done at the risk of endangering the life of the peaceful and law abiding citizens.
Criminal Code
Coming back to the death penalty itself, those who preach its abolition are doing so mainly in the name of respect for human life. They are right, life is a sacred thing, it comes from God, and criminals should begin by respecting it. Did Marcotte really have that respect when he retraced his steps to finish off police officer Brabant, already seriously injured?
What do you think of gang killings in the underworld, like the recent ones in the United States? We also have our own underworld in Canada, in Quebec. What about the fraudulent bankruptcies and the elimination of witnesses? We are not dealing with school children and I am not ready to say that they are all mental cases.
Mr. Speaker, I start from the principle that life is sacred and that it does for an individual to dispose of it. Whoever deprives another of his life is liable to lose his own. And I add that society, through the authority which comes to it from above, has the power and right to decide if such an individual deserves to live and how he must pay his debt to society.
I do not see in this statement anything to contradict the evolution principle in our civilization but rather a protection for that civilization.
I am conscious of the fact that in many cases there is need to ask oneself to what extent a murderer is responsible for his act. After the changes made in the law of 1961, I think we can leave it to our judicial system to define responsibility and to prove premeditation in cases of qualified murder. Most lawyers admit themselves that the danger of judicial errors is now eliminated by the changes made in the law. I do not accept either the argument that an individual who commits a murder is always in an abnormal state, it is too easy a way to make excuses for the murderers.
Mr. Speaker, I agree that we should endeavour to improve the world to the extent where capital punishment would no longer be required, but we have a long way to go. In my view, retention of the death penalty in the Criminal Code in no way interferes with the efforts already launched to rehabilitate criminals, to improve our social environment and to administer justice equitably.
Even with the eventual regression of crime, as a result of the evolution of social conditions and legislation, there will always be criminals. That is why I favour retention of

Criminal Code
capital punishment, if only to remind those who might feel inclined to make an attempt on their fellowman's life that they may be forced by society to forfeit theirs in return.

Mr. Speaker, this is an important topic, dealing as it does with the supreme and fundamental right: the right to live. The Declaration of Independence sets out that men are endowed by their Creator with certain inalienable rights, and among those are life, liberty and the pursuit of happiness.
Since the hon. member for Antigonish-Guysborough (Mr. Stewart) is not here, I thought I would get away with quoting that Republican document.
At some stages in our discussion we focus on the aspect of the right of life, so far as the accused or condemned is concerned. At other stages we concentrate on the right to live of his victims, actual and potential.
In any organized community as distinct from an anarchic state, the relation between the state and the individual is constantly of the essence. The right of the state to take life is precisely the question to which we must address ourselves as legislators in this debate. For that is the supreme assertion of the authority of the state, which represents the group, or the mass, against the individual.
I am very happy-and I hope I am not being naive in this-that there is to be a free vote. I think that one of the good legacies from this difficult era in our public life will be the greater degree of independence in the House of Commons on the many occasions when monolithic party solidarity and unity are at least unnecessary, and often unhelpful.
I do not pretend to specialist knowledge of this subject. Indeed, since it is a broad issue involving morals, ethics and the fundamental application of the rights of the state, and of the citizens to which the state belongs, I doubt if anyone can ground the certitude of his opinions upon the basis of esoteric knowledge. Not even lawyers, in my view, have any special pre-eminance in the solution of this very important question, because this is far more fundamental than the operation of the mechanics of the law, or the appraisal of an institution.
I confess that I enter the debate with a feeling far removed from supreme overconfidence in the rightness of my view. Over many years, both before and since leaving the halls of learning for the arena of politics, I
[Mr. Laniel.l
have studied, as much as I have been able to, the views of people who have written on this subject. Like many other hon. members, I have read reams of statistics.
Out of this experience, and out of my observation of Canadian conditions in this realm, I reluctantly confess that I cannot in conscience, and conscience here is our only and final guide, give my support to the abolitionist cause. I say reluctantly, because my basic emotional response and my sentiments all combine, if I may use that word-

-to incline me to oppose capital punishment. I therefore would designate myself as a non-dogmatic but convinced retentionist.
Very good.

I admire those who champion the abolitionist cause, although I note in passing that on this question on which public opinion seems so evenly divided the persuaders on the abolitionist cause seem to be heard much more in the land than those who with equal sincerity and after equally careful study and reflection support a different course.
[DOT] (7:50 p.m.)
Sometimes the retentionist is made to appear as a sort of hardhearted antediluvian who cares not for the feelings of his fellow man. Nor do I find myself impressed by the argument that the abolition of the death penalty is somehow synonymous with advancing civilization.
What is civilization? Is this not an area where we may make very subjective judgments not only from place to place, from community to community, but from age to age? In the present epoch the cultural group to which we belong in the western world seem to show an unprecedented regard for the sanctity of human life. We have vastly narrowed the grounds on which the state appropriately can take life. We have legislated against practices which shorten the life span, and we have made phenomenal advances in the war against fatal illnesses.
On the other hand, this same society has a technology which allows us to destroy one another, not in hundreds of thousands but in millions, and yet all of these developments are advances. So I cannot accept the suggestion that our advancing civilization must be assured and certified by the abolition of the state-imposed death penalty.

I listened with great pleasure and interest to the brilliant speech of the hon. member for Hochelaga (Mr. Pelletier), but even after having heard it I cannot find it in my heart to equate the abolition of capital punishment with such things as the discovery of America or the invention of the wheel.
Often it is said that it is morally wrong for the state to take life. Yesterday the hon. member for Kootenay East (Mr. Byrne) said:
I personally am unalterably opposed to the taking of life of any creature, either by an individual or by the state

-except unavoidably in self-defence, or to fulfil a need.

But it does strike me that when you erect moral postulates-

But once a moral postulate is erected it seems to me that the allowing for exceptions greatly undermines the moral position. To say that capital punishment is wrong, period, is a strong position. But once you argue that there are certain conditions, certain circumstances which justify death at the hands of the state, then you move the question from that of moral certainty to expediency, to utilitarianism. You ask, not is it right or wrong absolutely, but does this or that course serve best the interest of the state or of the individual.
Criminal Code
I think we get into much of our difficulty-and yet it is hard to keep out of this area-when we start to sort out kinds and degrees of murder, and begin to place different evaluations on the type of person murdered.
Those who are asked by the state to risk their lives in the care or incarceration of the criminal are placed by society in a most exposed position. They walk with peril daily. A penitentiary guard, a policeman, if they serve society's ends surely deserve society's special protection. I am much moved by the communications which I have received from members of this goup. They speak from an exposed position. They speak from a deep and awful awareness of the danger and when they write, as did the Civil Service Association of Canada not long ago, I cannot be cold to this kind of argument:
In the past years three penitentiary officers have lost their lives in Canadian federal penal institutions through inmate inspired disturbance or direct attack. Penitentiary officers feel that to remove the death penalty for murder committed under these circumstances would, in effect, remove the only deterrent to deliberate attacks on their lives.
I cannot be deaf to that kind of plea.
Other hon. members have developed the question of the life long sentence, the life sentence which is really for life. We all know, and society knows to its sorrow, that convicted murderers after serving a certain time have struck again at society after leaving the prison walls. And so some say, "Make a life sentence mean a life sentence." Others have already expressed their view on this. To make the life sentence a real life sentence removes all chance for rehabilitation, and knocks out completely all possibility of reform. It has already been described by others how life imprisonment itself is a living death. But the role of the prison guard in all of this is extremely dangerous.
I do not want to traverse the ground that has already been covered by some people who have gone over their 20 minutes. I hope I can finish within that limit, but the painful aspect for the sincere retentionist-and there is no monopoly of sincerity in this regard-is the awful possibility that an innocent man may be hanged. Regrettably this has happened. Legal institutions, like all human institutions, are fallible. It is a situation which would bring nothing but agony to anyone involved closely or remotely with such an irremediable and final miscarriage of justice.
But the anguish of those responsible for such an error as that, Mr. Speaker, would

March 24, 1968
Criminal Code
surely not be greater than that of those responsible for prematurely releasing upon society one who will again take the life of his fellows. Cases of this kind are, alas, far from uncommon.
Lord Justice Darling told a British House of Commons committee that 26 years experience on the bench had convinced him that in view of the checks and safeguards ef English law it is practically impossible for an innocent man to be hanged, although a great many guilty ones escape. But when the state itself allows a guilty one to escape to deal death again to a member of society, what then? Errors have been made.
Some people seem to believe that they can look at a man for a short while and know he is innocent. I do not have the omnicompetence to do that. I know psychiatrists can do much to reveal a man's mind but they cannot look into his heart and know exactly what is there. I say it is very hard to be sure and I would not want to be the one to take an unnecessary chance.
[DOT] (8:00 p.m.)
We hear much about statistics and we will hear more. I was very impressed by the statistics used by the hon. member for Lot-biniere (Mr. Choquette). I think, if we look at our own country and see what has happened here in recent years under the de facto abolition of the death penalty, we will find statistics there that are not overly cheering; in fact they are very disturbing. To me they seem to be going in the wrong direction; they are rising.
It has been said by those who dispute this point of view that you cannot make any short-range judgment, and that you must have a long time. But can those in charge of society's welfare and security take a long time? There have been highly civilized countries-to use that expression-which have abolished the death penalty and after careful consideration of the consequences of this action have reverted to it. It is not an easy question at all; far from it.
Like many other members I was present at the last two-day debate in 1960 on this question. I heard many fine speeches then. One which I remember very well is that of Mr. Martineau, a former colleague of mine. He said something which is very applicable today, when he pointed out as an absolute certainty that if that, particular bill were
[Mr. Macquarrie.l
voted down, not one additional murder would be committed.
But, how many hon. members who are listening to me here can say, consulting their own consciences, that if such a bill as this becomes law some murders which otherwise might not have been committed may be committed.
Let us search and consider that.
My learned friend from Royal said that there would be those who would quote scripture on all sides. That has been traditional. The clergymen in the south at the time of the civil war did quote many things in support of slavery, while their fellow theologians in the north found that the same doctrine gave them support.
No one has mentioned the Presbyterian church but, lest they think some Presbyterians base their views only on the grim Old Testament preachments, I would refer to a Presbyterian statement on the subject:
The right of the state to inflict capital punishment is currently being called into question.
That certainly is true.
Yet we would affirm the right of the civil magistrate to impose the death sentence for crimes like malicious and deliberate homicide. The state is given this right as the minister of God-
This is a reference to Romans 13: 1-7.
-and it shall have this right as long as evil continues to disturb the social order.
This is a religious statement, but I think it is a very meaningful observation of what we are facing up to today. So, Mr. Speaker, I am abridging my remarks in the hope that other speakers will have time. I can only say in conclusion, on the basis of careful thought, and in the hope that society might be a little safer, I feel it is in the public good that the law should remain as it is.

Might I ask a question, Mr. Speaker, of the hon. member who has just
spoken?

speakerposition: Deputy Speaker and Chair of Committees of the Whole of the House of Commons
speechtext:
Order. I understand that the time allotted the hon. member has expired.
The hon. member for St. Paul's.

Mr. Speaker, ever since the subject now before us was first raised, I have found it very difficult to decide just how I should vote on the question of the complete abolition of capital punishment. It is only very recently I have come to the conclusion, contrary to my original belief, that I must support this resolution.
March 24, 1966

Criminal Code
From the beginning I felt that capital punishment should be limited even more than it was by the amendment passed in 1961 which made the distinction between capital and non-capital murder. Nevertheless, for a long time I believed that capital punishment should be retained in certain circumstances; for example, pre-meditated murder for gain by a sane, sober adult, or the murder of a police officer or prison guard by a criminal in the course of committing a violent crime or while escaping or attempting to escape from prison.
Like other hon. members I have received a great deal of helpful correspondence from constituents and others and have been furnished with a great deal of informational material on the subject. After reading all of this and after discussing the matter with other members, and after listening to the debate in the house, I have, after considerable hesitation, come to believe that it is now possible for us to dispense completely with capital punishment, and that it is desirable we should do so.
Perhaps because of my own difficulty in reaching a decision, I fully appreciate the strength of the arguments which can be advanced in good faith by those who believe that capital punishment should be retained. For this reason, while I will vote for the complete and immediate abolition of capital punishment, I think it would be better to follow the procedure which was followed in England, namely to pass a statute suspending capital punishment for a trial period of five years.
During the last two and a half years the cabinet, by its policy of commutation, in effect has suspended capital punishment on its own responsibility. It would be much better for this house to provide specifically for the suspension of capital punishment for a five year trial period and remove this responsibility from the cabinet.
In this five year period I hope it will become apparent to an overwhelming majority of members that at our present stage of social development we safely can dispense with capital punishment. The necessary statute providing for permanent abolition can then be passed. If however, this hope proves ill-founded, then the present law providing for capital punishment will be reinstated automatically without further argument or debate.
I have said, Mr. Speaker, that I reached my conclusion only after a great deal of difficulty. Because I know some other members at
least have had the same difficulty, perhaps I may be permitted, at the risk of boring some, to retrace the tortuous course by which I reached the conclusion that contrary to my original belief I must support this resolution.
Like the rope itself, the case for capital punishment depends not upon the strength of a single strand, but upon the combined strength of a number of strands when entwined. All of us know, for example, and will have to admit, that capital punishment certainly serves one very fundamental principle of law in that it prevents repetition of the offence by the criminal; it is absolutely final and effective in this preventive function: this is one of the functions of punishment. I also believe that capital punishment has a somewhat greater deterrent effect than any sentence of imprisonment. I think each one of us can recognize this intuitively without reference to statistics.
[DOT] (8:10 p.m.)
Where there are so many variable factors involved, statistics are of doubtful value. If they are of any value, they merely indicate that the deterrent effect of capital punishment is not sufficiently great to make any very substantial difference in the rate of violent crime.
Capital punishment is also in accord with a basic feeling-perhaps a primitive one-that most of us have, that punishment should be in proportion to the seriousness of the crime. From this point of view, in executing a criminal, society does not show any lack of reverence for life. On the contrary, the execution of the criminal who has taken life without cause is meant to emphasize the reverence which society has for human life and the horror with which it regards the criminal act which destroys it.
The fact that certain other countries have abolished capital punishment is not really very helpful in view of the fact that many other countries retain it and, in any event, our circumstances in Canada may be different. Canada is a relatively young country with a relatively small and non-homogeneous population dispersed over a great area. We have very special problems in maintaining law and order, and we must find our own solutions to our special problems.
Nor do I believe that the issue before us can be resolved by reference to religious, philosophical or moral principles applied in the abstract. These principles must be applied, of course, but with specific reference to

March 24, 1966
Criminal Code
our actual circumstances in Canada today. Most of the great religions have recognized capital punishment in certain circumstances. Surely we must all recognize that it is impossible to say that capital punishment is immoral under all circumstances. In time of war or in a society emerging from disorder, or threatening to dissolve into disorder, or in a primitive society where other means of control and restraint are not available, capital punishment for the most violent crimes is probably essential.
I very much doubt that our ancestors were any more cruel than we are. The prevalence of capital punishment for a very large number of crimes just a hundred years or so ago is probably due to the fact that at that time society had not developed an effective prison system. In the absence of other means of preserving law, capital punishment was not immoral. On the contrary, it was essential, for, without law, society itself would perish.
It also seemed to me that arguments based upon the cruelty of hanging are really not relevant in this debate. If hanging is, in fact, cruel, surely less cruel methods of capital punishment could be developed. Nor do I place much stock in arguments based upon the fact that capital punishment is ignoble or degrading. Death is ignoble or degrading only if the cause of death is ignoble or degrading. The death of Socrates was not ignoble or degrading, nor was the death of Christ: tragic, yes, but not ignoble or degrading. Certainly the death of a murderer is ignoble and degrading, but it is so because of his crime, not because of the fact that society has executed him for that crime.
The argument that all criminals including murderers are ill or are the victims of society and should, therefore, be given medical and psychiatric care and attention can, I believe, be misleading. Some criminals may be insane or ill and they may respond to medical and psychiatric care; but there are other criminals who may be abnormal in the sense that they do not understand or respect the rights of others, or do not act or respond in a normal or socially acceptable way, but who are not ill in the sense in which we usually use that term. Even more important, in many such cases we have no reason to believe, in the present state of our knowledge, that their criminal abnormality, which is so dangerous to our fellow citizens and to society, can be cured by medical or psychiatric methods.

Nevertheless, while I appreciate the strength of all these arguments, I have come to the conclusion that I should support the abolition of capital punishment although, as I have said, I would prefer to see parliament suspend it for a trial period of five years.
At one time I was also inclined to think that there should be no possibility of parole in the case of a murderer who commits a premeditated murder for gain. I have since come to the conclusion that if it is believed he can be rehabilitated, the hope of parole should be extended even to him. Possibly also a life prisoner with hope of parole is less likely to kill a prison guard or commit a serious offence in prison if he has that hope of parole.
The resolution before the house suggests that parole should not be granted in these cases unless approved by the cabinet. I have some doubt as to whether this is desirable. I would have thought it better to impose final responsibility on the parole authorities and, if any review is considered desirable, it should not be by the cabinet but by a special board having specialized experience and knowledge in the field.
In abolishing capital punishment we must recognize the very heavy responsibility we are imposing upon our judicial and parole officers in trying to decide which offenders respond to rehabilitative treatment and which do not. We must be prepared to accept the fact that at the present stage of our knowledge, there are some offenders who cannot be rehabilitated and who will have to be imprisoned indefinitely. We who support abolition cannot have it both ways. If we want to abolish capital punishment we must be prepared to accept the fact that offenders who are incurable must be detained indefinitely in maximum security institutions, and possibly in special detention units of those maximum security institutions.
In making a decision to abolish capital punishment, we are imposing certain risks on society. We are imposing risks upon those who must work with the prisoners and we are imposing some risk on fellow citizens who must live in the immediate vicinity of the institutions in which dangerous criminals are confined.
Mr. Speaker, the governing principle which determined my decision in this debate is this. The purpose of our society should be to preserve and advance human life. It must be prepared to take life but only when necessary to protect other individuals or society itself.
March 24. 1966

In conformity with this principle, history appears to record a gradual movement away from capital punishment in peaceful and well-ordered countries as they mature and as they develop alternative methods of effective control.
In primitive societies, in impoverished societies which have not developed or cannot afford effective institutions for detention and correction, or in countries at war or faced with serious disorder, capital punishment is no doubt necessary, and indeed inevitable. The real question then facing us is one of judgment. Have we in Canada reached the point where we can now abolish the capital punishment of criminals without imposing undue risks upon other citizens and society itself? Clearly this is a question on which responsible and intelligent people, acting in good faith, can have very different opinions. That is why there is such a difference of opinion in Canada which, in turn, is reflected in differences of opinion among the members of this house.
Canada has developed a wealthy, complex and relatively mature society. I believe we can afford a multitude of institutions to deal in an appropriate manner with the great variety of offenders inevitable in a complex society. We can afford to provide medical and psychiatric care for those criminals who will respond to known methods of treatment. We can afford to establish institutions or special detention units from which there can be no parole or escape for murderers who do not or cannot respond to rehabilitative treatment.
[DOT] (8:20 p.m.)
I am happy that the decision was made to have this debate on the resolution before us and not on a detailed bill. As many of my constituents have pointed out, the issue of capital punishment should really not be considered in isolation or out of context. Instead this debate should give rise to a reconsideration of the much broader social questions relating to crime and punishment and rehabilitation. As was pointed out in a newsletter from the John Howard Society of Alberta, we should consider the lack of psychiatric and other rehabilitative treatment and perhaps, indeed, the complete investigation and reform of our penitentiary system and penal practices.
For example, one of my constituents has suggested that benefits might accrue to society and to the prisoner himself if he were made to do productive work for fair wages
Criminal Code
and use such wages to help pay his keep and contribute money to persons he had injured. I am told this has been done for years in Minnesota. There is other experience we could draw upon and many worth-while possibilities we could explore.
Earlier this month the appointment of a parliamentary committee on penitentiaries was authorized. I suggest, Mr. Speaker, that the authority of this committee should be widened to consider the broader problems to which I have referred and which cannot possibly be debated here at this time. However, the deliberations of any such committee should not be permitted to prejudice or delay the present resolution, which I hope will be supported by a large majority of members from every party in the house.

Mr. Speaker, more than one person who has spoken in this debate has said that, while listening to all the various speeches, he has not yet been convinced. I have been struck by the fact that in many ways what we have in this exercise is not really a debate, inasmuch as we are not taking close note of the various arguments that are presented and then weighing them to find how they equate with our own points of view. If I am looking for a serious and lively discussion on this issue, I merely have to retire a few feet behind this curtain and thereupon jeopardize all my opinions and ideas. It seems that to deal with what appears to be a highly insoluble problem we should all retire behind the curtain until we have reached a decision and then come forward and announce the result.
I may not have too many opportunities -indeed, I hope I shall not have too many opportunities-to disagree with my hon. colleague from the constituency of Queens (Mr. Macquarrie), I find that in this particular debate I am in considerable disagreement with him. The hon. member began his remarks by saying that surely a fundamental question to be raised here is the right of the state to take life. I do not think this is the fundamental question. The fundamental question on the part of the state is the necessity to take life. That, to me, is indeed the question we should be wrestling with in this forum.
I hope that in the course of my remarks I may say very clearly what is to me a position that has grown out of a number of years of association with those to whom we refer generally as criminals. I might say that I have probably spent more time behind bars

March 24. 1966
Criminal Code
and in prison than any other member in this house, and I am somewhat proud to make that assertion.
You are not that old.

An hon. member says that I am not that old. Age does not have too much to do with it. During my years at theological college I was fortunate enough to be prison chaplain. There I became acquainted in a very close way with a number of people who had been convicted of a variety of offences all the way up to and including murder. At a later date I was fortunate enough to visit, in the city of Chicago, a halfway house to which for further reformation some of the most incorrigible and dangerous offenders had been released after serving sentences. In all my experience with a variety of criminals it became obvious to me that many of the superficial conclusions we have drawn about people who commit criminal offences are highly incorrect.
I believe there are far too many of us in this house who make an easy division between those who are involved in some kind of crime, no matter what that crime may be, and ourselves. There is no such easy black and white division in humanity. Those who run afoul of the law, those who inhabit our various prisons and penitentiaries, are really not that much different from ourselves. The various motivations for their crimes are part and parcel of the same motivations that we experience daily, and we must try to do a much better job of understanding how they arrived in such an unfortunate position.
Hear, hear.

One of the arguments that has been used, and will be used, is this kind of indefinite referral from time to time to moral law. Very often in backing up such references to the moral law there is referral to the scripture. In my profession I must admit that I am not unfamiliar with various portions of the scripture, but I often find that in dealing with people who like to quote scripture a little knowledge is a dangerous thing.
Often people who desire to do so can find a text in the Old or New Testament to support their position, and they use this text as a proof text, out of context on a pretext. That is the kind of distortion of Biblical text that I am not going to tolerate. If I had the time, which I have not because Mr. Speaker will not allow it, I could prove almost anything by

the use of various scriptural texts. It is not this kind of isolated quotation from here and there that proves any position to be the right and infallible one. If one wants to make a serious appraisal of the scripture and the Christian position he should examine the total text.
What are the overriding and fundamental assertions of Christianity? If you take a serious approach to this question you will find, I think, that the teachings and practices of Our Lord and His followers was much different, in terms of His attitude to the criminal and social offenders, than we are often inclined to believe from these various texts that are hurled at us.
I shall not at this point make use of a variety of texts to prove what to me is a fundamental and overriding concern of the Christian gospel, that of acceptance, forgiveness and love. This was ultimately proved by Christ's own handling of those who were criminal offenders at the time of His own execution. One of the concerns that is uppermost in the minds of all of us, or it should be, is indeed the protection of society; and truly it has been stated that one of our fundamental, if not the most fundamental, concerns here is that society is truly protected.
When you come to the question of the protection of society, the arguments often go something like this: We do not really know what dangers we will be introducing to society by abolishing the death penalty; we do not want to take the risks of doing away with that protection and inflict untold misery on people in our society. That is the argument, is it not? But what of the other side of that argument? May there not be some dangers to society in retaining the death penalty?
[DOT] (8:30 p.m.)
What proof has been advanced in this house that retaining the death penalty will provide some increased advantages to our society? Should we not be fair and ask the question: Do we perpetrate, continue and prolong harm to society by retaining the death penalty? Surely, if one side of that question can be asked, the other side should be asked as well. The burden of the proof has, by and large in our particular time, been upon the abolitionist. Let us hear, then, from those who defend retention. I feel, as the hon. member for Queens said, that the abolitionists have been speaking much more because they have something definite and conclusive to say.
March 24, 1966

314?
Surely, if we are concerned about the protection of society, it is primarily a custodial concern. If you are going to advance the argument that by having the death penalty as a deterrent you are now protecting society, then let us revert to those golden, bygone days when we could execute people for the merest kind of social offence. Nobody would accept that position today. Then why should we accept the assertion that capital punishment is proper for one kind of crime but not for another? We are I submit illogical at that point.
There is, in our concern here, that great question of deterrence. Time and again it has been raised, and I am sure it will continue to be raised until the conclusion of this debate. At rock bottom, the thing which prevents us from removing capital punishment is the thought that somehow or other, it is going to deter a man who is contemplating a certain crime if he realizes that the penalty for it will be capital punishment. Is it a deterrent? I can say, as a result of having spoken to many hundreds of people for hours in prisons, that I have yet to meet one man behind bars who even intimated to me that the fear of the punishment he would receive for his offence would have in any way prevented him from committing it. Indeed most offenders with whom I have talked said it never even entered their minds. I have yet to meet an offender who did not say: I never expected to be caught. These men did not expect to be caught. When these people commit crimes, does anyone believe they are going to take the time to think of what the consequences of their acts might be from the standpoint of the administration of justice?
When we talk about fear as a deterrent, we must also ask the other question: Is it possible that fear of the death penalty may, for some people at some time, be a compulsion to commit a capital crime? I feel that at times it has been. A man has recently written a book that has gained quite a bit of popularity. His name is Bill Sands. Some of you may have read the book which is titled, "My Shadow Ran Fast". Mr. Sands is not a man who committed the ultimate offence, but is a man who has spent many years in notorious prisons, one of the major ones being San Quentin. He knew men who had committed terrible crimes. Caryl Chessman was one of his acquaintances. He said in his book and in public interviews that he found men behind bars who were saying that this business of being locked up like an animal was so bad, so
Criminal Code
meaningless an existence, that they would be willing to take a chance on murdering, either a fellow prisoner or a guard so they would be quickly and speedily dispatched from this world.
Let us not think that by keeping the death penalty and locking men up in our institutions year after year we are protecting our prison guards. At times we may be doing the reverse of that. More than one prisoner behind bars today will tell you that he would much rather find a way to end his life quickly than to drag out this kind of meaningless existence. There is a great deal that needs to be done within our whole penal system, a system that we think is effective. We talk time and again about how valuable the fear of punishment is in the protection of society. If the fear of punishment is effective, I ask this question: Why is it that more than two thirds of those who are serving in our penitentiaries at this moment will, in all likelihood, return after their release, having committed other crimes? Does that sound like protecting society by some sensible kind of institutionalized justice? I think it is an atrocity that we put up with this kind of inferior system. Surely we should give much greater consideration to the fact that it may well be that the fear we are creating may do more harm in our society, may create more social hostility, than any danger that would be involved in the removal, once and for all, of the method of capital punishment.
Now, I suppose I have been fairly emotional in this debate. I am an emotional person at times. We have been told by the press that we were going to have an emotional debate, so we do not want to let the press down. Why is it we are having an emotional debate? Surely this should not be that emotional an item. Rarely have we dealt with such an issue which involved so few people. This is such an emotional question that it is not wise to get behind the curtain if you do not want to become involved in one of these emotional debates.
Why is it an emotional debate? Is it because of a tremendous feeling of antipathy, a sense of revenge, which we feel when a particularly horrible crime is committed? We want to see that person get what is coming to him. Is it also because of the fact there is a presupposition throughout our whole social organization that in order to control the relationship of men in our society we must always have in the background some certain element of fear? Far too much of our social

March 24, 1966
Criminal Code
control is registered at the level of fear. It is a sad sort of thing, I think, that we have come to accept this as a fact, that the instrument of fear must be used in working out ways for our society to control our comings and goings, our human patterns in society.
I am even somewhat dissatisfied with this motion which is before us. I feel that the movers of this resolution have their feet in both worlds. They are against capital punishment but they have also put in that safeguard of life imprisonment. In other words, they are doing away with one fear deterrent and putting another in its place. Surely some time in our society we must come to the point where we can free these fear ridden, hostile people who offend our society and control them by some other means than blind punishment and directed social hostility. I hope the time has come when we can take some positive action in this regard. The hon. member for St. Paul's (Mr. Wahn) has suggested that perhaps we are not quite ready to take the risks the hon. member for Hochelaga (Mr. Pelletier) urged us to strive for today. Perhaps we will have to adopt the British solution of a five year period in which we really give this thing a test. I would vote for that, because at least we would be making a step in the right direction. I cannot vote for anything less than that, really, because the retention of capital punishment in any form, for any criminal offence whatever, is in effect saying that the retention of capital punishment is a right and proper system for our society. I cannot agree with this.
I hope that we are in a period where we can accept what I believe the majority of opinion of this country has accepted in a passive way for the past three years. I hope we can take enough responsibility, show enough desire in this house to be in favour of something that says something tremendously important about the dignity of each and every individual and his relationship to his fellow man.
[DOT] (8:40 p.m.)

Mr. Speaker, I do not intend to be very long, but I wish to indicate clearly what stand I shall take, as other members will, when the time comes to vote on the matter now before us.
Naturally, we are discussing a disturbing, emotional matter; I might even say that while participating in such a debate, there is somehow a feeling that one's neck is in the noose.

Nevertheless, most of the speakers who spoke before me managed to come through with flying colours, and I feel I should have no difficulty in expressing my opinion on the matter.
However, I am in a slightly difficult situation. I have, as many other members, made several inquiries in my riding, in the last few months, indeed for over a year now, inviting my constituents to let me know how they feel about this debate, that is, the abolition or retention of capital punishment.
The response of my constituents has not been very strong; in fact, the percentage was very small. I do not know whether they were embarrassed to speak, or what else. At any rate, if I had considered only the letters I received, the decision would have been that much easier. But I felt among the people of my riding and among the people of the province of Quebec a certain reticence to depart from this system of justice called capital punishment.
Then, of course, I thought of the attitude I should take myself and I came to the conclusion that I had no other alternative. There may be some who would be inclined to fear that in taking position against such a measure, perhaps against the will of the people they represent, they might commit political suicide. At any rate, I believe it would be preferable to make known my position because if I did not act as I do, I would feel guilty of betraying the sacred principles supported by the most unfaltering and most serious beliefs.
Of course, there might be a very easy way out: one could sit in one's place, let the others do the talking and when the time comes to vote, go along with the majority. Or again, if I had simply followed the desire which may not have been sufficiently expressed by the people of my riding, but which I think I detected, I could have said: "Well, I rely on what the people of my riding have told me." But I refuse to play the part of Pontius Pilate and wash my hands of it all, hiding behind the feelings of the population which might not be sufficiently well informed regarding the problem we are discussing today. Therefore, I refuse to play the part of Pontius Pilate, and in a debate of this kind, I must make my opinion known freely, sensibly, honestly and conscientiously, facing up to my own responsibilities, according to my conscience, in that respect.
Naturally, I may say that I have great respect for the opinions which have been
March 24, 1966

expressed but I do not share the same views; I respect somebody else's opinion because any human being has a right to his own opinions and I make a duty of respecting this right which is one of the most sacred to man.
I should wish, however, that a greater number of people would get more information and more literature concerning abolition or retention of the death penalty, as I had time to do myself and, no doubt, most of the representatives of different counties of this country in this house for the past two or three years. If more people had been able to become informed in this way, it would be perhaps easier for them, thanks to references which would enlighten them on the situation, to express their feelings in this house.
My interest in this matter is not recent, because several years ago already I was closely interested on account of my work at that time as a news commentator on radio and television in a crime, a legal case, a trial which made the rounds of the legal circles in Quebec city, and since I did not live very far from where the alleged crime had been committed, I followed the case closely. I was a little excited to see how the case had been dealt with; as a matter of fact, it came up again not so long ago, and it raised doubts among the people on various aspects of justice. And, of course, I also discussed with learned colleagues, lawyers-a profession which I respect, I wish to add in passing- but I cannot agree with what some of them told me and what has been repeated here: If you were a lawyer, if you ever had to plead some cases. I repeat, with all due respect to the honourable members of the legal profession, that I cannot agree that it is an over-riding criterion for a better assessment of the case for the retention or the abolition of capital punishment, for, in my opinion, the spirit, or if you prefer, the concept of justice does not necessarily require legal knowledge or great legal know-how to express itself. It is something that is felt, it is something which has to do with the heart and the spirit, and I believe that any right-minded person is also in a position to form an objective opinion on such matters.
It is not necessary to let ourselves be mesmerized by high-sounding words such as criminology, penology, psychology and so on. We must consider the matter objectively.
Looking at the members gathered in this house, I ask those who have made up their minds and those who may still be in doubt
Criminal Code
what would be their reaction if they were called upon, let us say tomorrow, to sit on a jury who would have to decide whether a fellow human will live or will have to forfeit his life. Perhaps, in this way they would see whether they could express their views with as much ease. They would have to face the learned and moving pleas of counsel for the defence and of the prosecutor who seek, each in his own way, to impress those men or women that have been selected to decide the issue.
I had an opportunity to attend a number of trials, and that is roughly what I witnessed, It was claimed that people who could afford it made sure to retain the services of a skilled criminal lawyer to defend them.
I even saw one of our great criminal lawyers of the province of Quebec defend a poor chap accused of manslaughter; he felt so secure that he was sleeping in the dock. He said: My lawyer will fix it up for me. As a matter of fact, everything went well, but this cannot always be expected. At some trials, one may wonder, for instance, whether there should not rather be some equality, when one sees the difference between the amounts spent by the crown to prosecute the offender, and by the accused; if the latter has rather limited means, there is then a disparity which, in my opinion, is not normal. That is why, when one often attends trials, one wonders, if the man could afford one of the most outstanding criminal lawyers, whether he would not stand a better chance of having his case settled, of saving his life, of escaping the noose. This is a further reason which prompts me to speak in favour of the abolition of the death penalty.
Now, the death penalty itself has been referred to on several occasions and in various ways. Is it really an effective deterrent? That is the point. There is surely room for doubt. Can it be asserted that the threat of the death penalty has ever prevented anyone from committing murder? Surely not. Many instances, many quotations could be given.
And then, why all this secrecy surrounding the death of a criminal if it is to be used as a deterrent? In certain African countries, in Saudi Arabia, I believe, not only is the law of retaliation applied, but rather barbarous punitive measures are also taken.
For theft, for instance, they are satisfied simply to cut off the hand of the thief in the public square. I grant you it is rather radical, but it seems that it works out there. Nevertheless, these are barbaric methods, but

this represents somewhat a shameful execution, because in the system we know today an execution is carried out on the sly, generally after the twelve strokes of midnight.
The trial is public, the sentence is public, but when the time set for the execution comes around, it is carried out before a few select witnesses in the small hours. How do you think this can deter? And what results can it have on a criminal who may be recognized as such at a later date?
If punishment were to be meted out in public, as it used to be, there could be grounds for discussion. In any event, I too agree that the criminal should be in a position not to do any harm. Abolition deserves a try.
