Obviously, there is nothing perfect on this earth. Society will always be imperfect. Punishment will always have to be meted out. It seems this is a hard fact of our social life. But capital punishment produces no good; everyone is aware of it, everyone admits it. It makes the condition of man more distressing than it need be. The fate of man will be no worse if capital punishment is abolished.
These are great hopes that abolition will improve society. Nothing is lost through abolition of capital punishment, society is not being jeopardized in any way. It may be, and I was most interested by the opinions of the previous speaker, that we will do some little good in working at finding other solutions to this problem. Mr. Speaker, we should stop to consider the root of the evil. Who is truly responsible? Perhaps we should not always punish those who disobey the law. Most criminals today are the victims of a still badly-organized society which has been unable, in the 20th century, to clear away its many slums. There are also other reasons. Let us not forget that many were taught to kill in cold blood-those who fought in world conflicts, who were in the Korean war, for example.
There are also deficiencies at home, parents who are too often irresponsible. There are many factors: the unhealthy climate of our penitentiaries and other institutions where criminals are further taught the ways of crime rather than rehabilitated- where young prisoners are perverted by older ones. These are also sources of evil and they too should be dealt with.
It is all very well to say that we should continue along the present lines, but we should look around us and strike at the root of the

evil. It is the evil itself that must be cured. It is not simply a question of legal murder by hanging, the electric chair or the gas chamber. All these things should be studied, all the more so because there are many other reasons for a deeper and more appropriate study.
And when you look at the roots of the evil, you see a spread of firearms. You can get them with the greatest of ease. There is also television which spoils many of our young people, who are watching programs that are surely unsuitable. At Christmas, when gifts are received, most toys are murderous weapons such as guns and revolvers. Kids learn at a tender age.
Everything should be examined and, as I said, we should go directly to the source of evil. Obviously, I cannot personally endorse the statement found on page 60 of the English version of the white paper on capital punishment sent to us by the Minister of Justice:
The fact that there was no known Canadian instance of the execution of an innocent person indicated the effectiveness of present procedures by way of trial and executive review and this suggests that the risk of error does not present a reasonable argument for abolition in Canada.
Many members who have spoken before me had the opportunity to take a stand on that. Yet, it seems to me that there have been such instances. In Quebec city, many years ago, a nephew was hanged for the murder of his aunt but his uncle, on his deathbed -I do not remember his name and I was thinking of Giroux, but I do not know-confessed that he himself had killed the old aunt. He recovered his health and he has not been seen since.
This is just a case I am referring to in passing. There are others that raised many comments and made the headlines. In my opinion, the case of Wilbert Coffin was never clearly settled. It was discussed and will keep on being discussed for many years. Other cases were also submitted by the other hon. members.
So, there still remains the possibility of mistakes. These could be eliminated, and in a most simple way.
Obviously, there are certainly improvements to be brought about before taking perhaps such a decision. The Criminal Code should be amended. There will surely be amendments proposed to the National Parole

There might be some way also to proceed with justice itself. I understand that loathsome crimes are committed and that may be why a definite hesitation to do away with this medieval system of capital punishment seems to be felt in the province of Quebec at present. Well, several cases occurred, as was said by several people, and that is when emotions became involved. I understand there is the Marcotte case, and the Santa Claus case, there is the Dion case; these are very sad, obviously.
But if the workings of justice are examined in these cases, there may also be improvements to be made. It seems to me, and I am not so well informed on legal matters, I admit, I am not a lawyer, it seems to me very strange that in the Marcotte case, for instance, there were three persons involved. Fournelle, the accomplice, was taken aside and told: "You are going to help us. You are going to tell on your partner in crime and if you tell us, you will save your life."
What do we do, then, with a gangster who is as guilty as his partner if not more, who may also have done the shooting? By letting him think that his life will be spared, we make him perhaps not more of a criminal than he was, but more base and vile, since he will be used to prove his companion's guilt. And what will happen to him? He will be sentenced to some years or a lifetime in prison, but his life will be spared and he will be used against the other culprit.
It seems to me that such deals have no place in today's society. That is another reason why I go on record as in favour of the abolition of the present system.
You know that a dangerously close margin separates revenge from punishment in the

For those who had an opportunity to read a bountiful literature, for instance for those who are interested in birds, there was a prisoner known as the Birdman of Alcatraz, who wrote marvellous things about birds while in prison. Several generations of young and older people are taking advantage today of his masterly research.
Many have certainly had the opportunity to read books by Caryl Chessman, this American whose death sentence was commuted several times before he was finally executed. He had already begun to make a fine contribution.
I heard some mention that in a few years when psychology will have made some progress, it would perhaps be advisable to deal again with this matter and to consider then the opportunity of abolishing capital punishment.
Therefore, while we are waiting for science to develop and for us to become more intelligent, all we have to do, it seems, is to wait. It seems to me that such an attitude means: Let us remain barbarians, wait until science has made further progress; then we shall become more human again. This is, perhaps, too strong a language, but, obviously, it reflects, in a way, the views of many people.
Consequently it seems to me there is surely a way of ending this practice described by many, and I am one of them, as meaningless in the modern world.
I do not intend to quote the Bible. On the other hand, it is amazing that so many denominations have drawn from it for all the literature that we have received. The majority of people, those who belong to Christendom, seem to share the opinion that the time has come to show a little more respect for human life and to put an end to those executions that can no longer be justified in this twentieth century. I do hope that by the end of this debate, many will keep on looking for information, reading the documents they received and discussing with friends and fellow citizens-two heads are better than one- and that we shall find all together the best solution, the most desirable one, which will provide for the upholding of law, order, and authority.

I might add that the statement he quoted is the only official statement of the Presbyterian church in Canada on the question of the death penalty, but recently this has been under review, and the 91st General Assembly appointed a special committee in 1965 to consider this question and report to the 92nd General Assembly in June, 1966. Therefore it seems to me that the Presbyterian Church in Canada is looming in the direction of the abolition of the death penalty, and I think the hon. member for Queens would permit me to add that to the statement he quoted.
This afternoon the hon. member for Swift Current-Maple Creek (Mr. McIntosh) prefaced his remarks by saying he was taking the position taken by the young Conservatives with regard to the retention of capital punishment. concerning the position of young people with regard to the abolition of capital punishment.
Today all members of the house received a copy of a letter from the Student Christian Movement which reads:
The Student Christian Movement in the University of Toronto has asked me to express its concern with respect to the forthcoming motion and debate on capital punishment. The cabinet of the S.C.M., after much thought and discussion on the subject, has recorded its unanimous disapproval of such a penalty, no matter what the crime, and its decision is based on all grounds, both moral and objective. The letter was signed by the president of the Student Christian Movement.
There are two aspects of capital punishment with which I would like to deal. The first is the religious view, the position that a religious person may take, based on his religious faith. The second aspect is the question of compensation for victims of criminal violence, and in particular for the widows and dependents of victims of the crime of murder.
Concerning the religious view there is a great diversity of thinking among Christians on the question of capital punishment. All of us have received letters from individuals, and briefs from organizations, setting forth their different views. I think it is fair to say that most Protestant churches favour abolition, with a few fundamentalists disagreeing with the general view. Roman Catholics in the main agree with abolition, and I was deeply impressed with a lecture given by Father Kelly, president of St. Michael's College in Toronto, before the Society for Abolition of Capital Punishment. I ask your indulgence, Mr. Speaker, to quote some parts of his speech. He said:
The voice of Protestant ministers and Jewish rabbis has been heard. If the Roman Catholic voice has been heard, it has generally been the voice of Catholic laymen. I feel obliged to be here because I think it necessary to add at least one Roman Catholic priest's voice to the crusade . . .
The first point I should like to make is that I see no theological or moral basis for retention and I see both theological and moral reasons for abolition . . .
Now it seems to me that punishment is by definition retributive; it pays back irrespective of the intention of the authority which imposes it. The big question is whether some substitute for capital punishment pays back enough. At this point another necessary consideration intervenes: a human punishment must always be directed to the good of society. A punishment which would prejudice rather than promote the good of society is plainly not a just punishment irrespective of the guilt of the offender or the authority of the punisher. The point I am trying to make here is that it is seriously questionable whether retribution alone ever provides a

sufficient motive for punishing. If I seem to labour this point it is simply because the die-hard reten-tionists are not satisfied when the obvious lack of reform necessarily implied by the death penalty is buttressed by the proof that capital punishment is no deterrent to the so-called capital crimes. The die-hard retentionist comes back to the argument on retributive grounds, and retributive grounds alone. He comes back to the point where it seems to me he must logically insist that inflicting suffering on an offender is justified in itself, an end in itself, regardless of the consequences whether they be good or bad. The crime seems to him to warrant pain and the degree of pain is determined by the gravity of the offence. Vindication is made a sovereign and self-justifying end. The modern conscience rejects this and I think that on this point the modern conscience is right.
He continues:
The death penalty is obviously not adapted to purposes of reform. This element can in no way be suggested as a justification for retention of capital punishment. Neither can retribution. The "life for a life" appeal is made on emotional rather than rational grounds. It is rather curious that this is the only instance in modern law where we try still to maintain a perfect matching of the crime and the punishment for it. If one man stabs another we do not insist on stabbing him in return; if he victimizes another by perjury, we do not in turn victimize him by perjuring him. The "life for a life" may have the appearance of justice but it is appearance only. To object that the indignation of society at an act of murder is different from and needs an expression different from that shown toward other crimes puts the burden of proof on the objector. Death of the offender is not the only way of expressing indignation. Whether it is the most practical way can be decided only on the basis of empirical investigation. This is precisely the area in which it has been demonstrated beyond any reasonable doubt that the death penalty for murder does not achieve the ends alleged for having it in our law books; it does not reform; it does not deter; it is purely vindictive and, as such, does society no good at all.
[DOT] (9:10 p.m.)
It is not the only way or even the best way of upholding the divine law and it does not promote human betterment. The empirical evidence available to us in this moment in history does not allow a case to be made for retaining capital punishment for murder nor for maintaining that it is the only or best way of registering our indignation at those who take the lives of others.
I would also like to note, Mr. Speaker, that the Vatican state retains the death penalty but no longer carries out executions. Indeed the Pope frequently appeals for clemency. I recall attending Holy Blossom Temple in Toronto in the fall of 1964 where I heard Rabbi Powell give the position of the Jewish faith with regard to the abolition of capital punishment. He stated that although the Old Testament calls for the death penalty, there was abundant evidence in the Talmud which supported abolition, and indeed the Jewish faith has taken this position.
Criminal Code
The religious persons in favour of retention of the death penalty use mostly selected Old Testament texts with an occasional New Testament text to support their position. This is a wrong approach to the problem. What we are called upon to do is to strive for that mind which was in Jesus Christ and to bring it to bear upon the issues of our time. The New Testament gives us much guidance on the problem, not in the form of a set of answers, but in developing an attitude and a concern to find the ways and means of loving God with our whole being and our neighbour as ourselves. Slavery is an issue which provides an example. There is no specific Bible text prohibiting slavery, yet when we take the Bible as a whole and strive to walk by the spirit, slavery is unjust and evil. So with capital punishment. We should not approach these issues by asking what this verse or that verse says, but by bringing an elightened and compassionate conscience to the issues. It is not what the Bible says in this specific verse, literally interpreted, but what it says to us through its total message interpreted in terms of today's conditions that is relevant.
To take a Christian approach, Mr. Speaker, we must find out what is the situation. We must see what is wrong and use our best reasoning to deal helpfully and effectively with the problem, always keeping in mind the social ethic of reverence for life. Therefore, a necessary part of the Christian approach is to discover how capital punishment works out. We have had difficulty since 1961 because of the distinction between capital and non-capital murder, and the statistics have been rather difficult to interpret. However, in recent years the average number of convictions for murder in the United States has been slightly more than 8,500 and the average number of executions has been slightly less than 35. The statistics show with remarkable unanimity that neither the presence of the death penalty nor the frequency of the executions acted as a deterrent to murder. As it is now applied the death penalty is nothing but an arbitrary discrimination against an occasional victim. The victims tend to be selected on a very emotional basis in which the prejudices of society find expression.
The great majority of executions are of persons who, because of ignorance, poverty or other reasons, are unable to secure adequate legal counsel for themselves, while criminals of a higher economic or social status find

March 24, 1966
Criminal Code
legal means for evading execution. The possibility of the death penalty can influence jurys to acquit persons actually guilty of murder, thus contributing to the miscarriage of justice. So long as they are administered by fallible human beings, courts will be subject to error. All other judicial errors, upon discovery, in some measure can be corrected and repaired; a judicial error culminating in an execution, however, is totally irreparable.
Without minimizing justice, the Christian must find his answer to the problem in compassionate concern. This is not sentimental romanticizing over a criminal, but a recognition that since man was made in the image of God, his life and blood are sacred, and that the major concern is his rehabilitation. Vengeance must give way to forgiveness and reconciliation. This means that the primary concern of correctional institutions is rehabilitation and restoration based upon informed compassion and humane wisdom.
The Christian has a continuing task of interpreting to the community the kinship of all human beings, and the depth of our concern is based on the fact that he is a human being and our brother under one God and Father of us all.
The second aspect I am going to deal with, Mr. Speaker, is compensation for victims of criminal violence. In murder cases there usually is a proper and deep public concern for the families of the victims. The loss of the head of a family results, among other things, in serious financial hardship for the widow and dependant children. The community must show as much, if not more, concern for the widow and the dependants for the loss suffered as it does for the reformation and rehabilitation of the offender.
In England a white paper on compensation for victims of crimes of violence was approved by way of motion on May 5, 1964 by the House of Commons and on May 7 by the House of Lords whereby a criminal inquiries compensation board was directed to be set up to compensate victims of criminal violence and which included compensation for the spouse or dependants of persons fatally injured.
This board operates in much the same manner as our workmen's compensation board, and in the case of a fatal injury any compensation awarded to the spouse or dependants is assessed on the same principles as a claim under the Fatal Accidents Act, except for a restriction in the calculation of the loss

of income of the deceased. This scheme is a major breakthrough in the development of our laws concerning victims who have suffered as a result of crimes. It is a recognition that not only must the offender be punished but, equally as important, the victim must be compensated. To my knowledge only England, New Zealand and California have introduced this type of legislation. Canada needs similar legislation and Canadians are entitled to demand it immediately in our move forward with our treatment of offenders for crimes.
May we be granted wisdom, vision and courage, Mr. Speaker, as we move forward in the full brotherhood of man and the fatherhood of God.

Mr. Speaker, I suggest it might be useful at this time if, for a moment or two we were to think about what we are being asked to do here tonight and what we have been asked to do in the last couple of days. It seems to me we are talking about the abolition of capital punishment when in effect capital punishment now has been almost abolished. The only area in which capital punishment now obtains is premeditated coldly calculated murder and also murder of some particular individuals, such as policemen.
The hon. member for Queens (Mr. Mac-quarrie) impressed me very much tonight when he said if we vote down this resolution Monday night not one additional murder will be committed; not one that is certain. If we do not, I will leave someone else to answer that question.
[DOT] (9:20 p.m.)
Mr. Speaker, my good friend the hon. member for Kootenay East (Mr. Byrne) said we should be Christ-like, and that we should in effect turn the other cheek. I suggest to him that the same Christ took a whip and drove the money changers out of the temple. He was not a namby-pamby.
The hon. member opposite, for whom I have the greatest respect, representing a Prince Edward Island riding the name of which I cannot remember, suggested, if in fact he did not state, that most of the criminals behind bars would prefer to hang rather than be imprisoned. I find that difficult to accept. I had a little to do with the commutation of one man's sentence of death to life imprisonment. It seemed to me that that man was very happy when he received this news.
March 24, 1966

I have heard it said by retentionists, of which I am one, not without some difficulty, that they base their conclusions on the fact that life ends at the grave. I cannot believe that because I do not believe life ends at the grave, and in that regard I am in very good company, including a succession of Popes, one of which was Pius XII. Another who believed as I was St. Thomas Aquinas.
I did not think I would have to refute a speech made by a Catholic priest, but someone had the courtesy to send me a copy of one made by Father Kelly. I do not intend to attempt to refute his speech at this time, but the quotation of the hon. member seemed to concentrate on retribution only. There are many other reasons for punishment and retribution. Surely the important part of punishment is its deterrent effect. I am not interested in retribution, as I hope I am not a very revengeful person.
One of the questions we have to ask ourselves is whether the death penalty is a deterrent, and would its removal be helpful in protecting innocent victims? It seems to me the essence of the abolitionists' case is the sanctity of human life. Yet it is for that very reason, the fact that I do value so highly the sanctity of human life, that I must oppose the complete abolition of the death penalty. I am concerned about convicted criminals, but I am far more concerned about the innocent victims and, above all, the possible future victims of criminals.
The ultimate justification of any punishment, Mr. Speaker, is not only that it is a deterrent, but that it is an emphatic denunciation by the community of a crime, and from this point of view there are some murders which, in the present state of public opinion, demand the most emphatic denunciation of all, namely the death penalty.
Saint Thomas Aquinas said, "The slaying of an evildoer is lawful inasmuch as it is directed to the welfare of the whole community". Every human being is a social being by nature, needing to live in society and not being self-sufficient. He cannot attain his perfection without the help of others.
Social living requires the setting up of a government and order. The government of a country has the right, indeed the duty, to do what is necessary to preserve social order and the well-being of its citizens. When any member of society commits such serious crimes as to be a menace to the community, I believe the government has the right to put him to death.

Criminal Code
It has been said that society is like a body with a head, and that if a member of the body becomes gangrenous it can be cut off, when necessary, to save the whole body. Of course only the government can administer capital punishment, having responsibility, indeed the duty, of safeguarding the community. I know the Bible gives us as one of the Ten Commandments of God: "Thou shalt not kill". But surely in its very context this refers to murder and unjust killing. It must be remembered that God also gave Moses the Jewish law which contained death as the penalty for several grave crimes.
An individual obviously is allowed to kill in self-defence if necessary. The state can also defend itself and the country in war when unjustly attacked, and can order its soldiers to kill. The state has done so and will do so. Likewise the state can kill an individual of its own if the individual is, indeed, a deadly enemy of society.
The fear of capital punishment should, and in my opinion does, deter many from serious crime. I feel that even though life imprisonment does stop this man, the convicted criminal, from further crime, it will not be sufficient to deter others. Capital punishment has been, as I said earlier, almost abolished in this country. I cannot agree in conscience that complete abolition is warranted.
Much of the opposition to the retention of capital punishment is based on the idea of the fallibility of a single jury in a murder trial, of the possibility of an inflamed atmosphere in which a trial might take place, and of the personal disposition of a single judge in directing the jury in such a trial. However, under the appeal provisions a person convicted of murder may appeal his conviction and, in the impartial atmosphere surrounding this court, he may have the conviction set aside with a judgment or a verdict of acquittal entered. He may be granted a new trial or he may have the capital charge reduced to a lesser crime, if the jury on the evidence could have found him guilty of such an offence. My observation and my experience is that murder trial juries demand the highest possible standards of proof. I suggest there is a natural human reluctance to bring in a guilty verdict. I know this from personal experience, having been a member of a murder trial jury. This is not a duty that one takes lightly. Nor do attorneys or judges take this duty lightly. No man on trial for murder is ever given a superficial trial. I feel therefore

March 24, 1966
Criminal Code
that there is little chance of an innocent man's being sentenced to death.
I want to add my voice to the growing number of Canadian citizens who feel that the innocent victims of violence, of murder and other crimes should be in some way compensated. Too long have we ignored the innocent victims of criminality. I am quite sure that members of parliament in all areas of this big land of ours have had experience in this matter and have constituents who have been, are being and will be victimized.
This government and all governments spend millions and million of dollars on crime prevention. Certainly this money is well spent on police protection and all the multifarious activities surrounding our protection. However, when all this police protection breaks down and a family is victimized by a murderer or other criminal, surely the state owes something to the victim or victims of its failure, in some cases-in many cases- widows and children. Just as society bears the responsibility for crime prevention, it seems logical to me that society should bear responsibility for its failure in crime prevention.
I should like to discuss one other point if I may, Mr. Speaker. Many times we have read in the newspapers, or realized through our own experience, that citizens have not come to the aid of policemen in certain instances. Indeed, it is a misdemeanour knowingly not to come to the aid of a policeman in the exercise of his duty. Yet when one does act as a citizen should and is injured or even killed in that endeavour, it seems to me there is little provision for the victim or for the family for injury or death caused in this way, no matter how heroic the action might be.
[DOT] (9:30 p.m.)
If this were done, if suitable and just provision were made, obviously it would provide the incentive for more volunteer action by ordinary citizens on the side of the law to help the police when they could. It seems to me, Mr. Speaker, that too often the personal plight of those involved has been ignored. I believe this should and must be remedied.
In this debate a moralist may argue that the state has no right to take away human life, for in so doing the state is playing God. Somebody once said, "Man must play God for he has acquired certain God-like powers, among them a considerable degree of mastery over life and death, and he cannot avoid that exercise." Science has put into our hands, and

politics has required us to grasp firmly, instruments that can affect the very image of man hundreds of years hence, and for that matter, the duration of all life.
In a less awesome, but awesome enough way, modern medicine has been usurping prerogatives once held to be God's alone. It has learned to cheat death, not merely by the prolongation of life but by calling men back to life after several hours on the other shore. The judge who orders an execution is no more guilty of playing God than the doctor who, having decided that a human being has been summoned to eternity too soon, restores him to this world of time, and often of suffering.
Any case for the retention of the death penalty does not rest upon sentiment or hysteria. It is based quite simply on the fact that, human nature being what it is, potential criminals are most effectively deterred from crime by what they fear most. The penalty of death is obviously the most dreaded punishment. It seems to me it is certainly more dreaded than life imprisonment. While saying this, Mr. Speaker, I am certainly not reasoning for the retention of the death penalty by hanging: Far from it. It is not for me to decide what form the death penalty should take. I suggest there are far more humane methods of execution than hanging. As I see it, there could hardly be a less humane method. However, the death penalty is a warning always there, always warning; just like a lighthouse throwing its beams out to sea. We hear about shipwrecks, but we do not hear much about the ships that the lighthouse guides safely on their way. We do not have proof of the number of ships it saves, but we do not tear down the lighthouse.
I am not one of those who believe that punishment alone promises social security. A year or so ago a minister of justice said:
Whenever public opinion sees only the horror of the criminal act and not the history of a delinquent soul, it naturally seeks merely to punish.
He went on to say that we must show Canadians how human conduct is moulded by poverty, sickness, mental deficiency, ignorance or a childhood marred by cruelty, hate, divorce and alcoholism. We must show the grotesque defamation of character which results from punishment which is blindly vengeful. We must show how human treatment, confidence and modern scientific care can salvage an individual, apparently criminal by nature, and return him to civil society transformed and grateful. This I believe, Mr. March 24, 1966

Speaker. But the law of love is also the love of liberty, and love and mercy have no stability without basic justice. Lowering the standards of justice is never a substitute for the concept of mercy. I find it only too easy to agree that the execution of a murderer is a horrible spectacle, but I insist that the murder of an innocent person by an atrocious crime is far more horrible. To love your neighbour is to protect him.
Some time ago in these parliament buildings there was a meeting of the attorneys general of our 10 provinces. I am informed that almost all those attorneys general-I believe with the exception of just one-agree that the retention of the death penalty is necessary, at least for atrocious crimes. These are men of long experience in justice, and with men and criminals of every type. It is their considered opinion that the stand I take here tonight-and not without a great deal of difficulty because certainly I am not, I hope, a particularly vengeful person-is the correct one; that is, that capital punishment should be retained at least for deliberate, despicable, atrocious murders deliberately planned and coldly committed.
After the most careful consideration, Mr. Speaker, I have reached the conclusion that I cannot in all conscience vote for the complete abolition of the death penalty.

Mr. Speaker, I rise on a question of personal privilege. When the hon. gentleman who has just resumed his seat rose to speak, I applauded him most vigorously. I was misinformed. I understood he was opposed to capital punishment. I now wish to recall that applause.

speakerposition: Deputy Whip of the Liberal Party; Chief Government Whip's assistant; Deputy Chair of Committees of the Whole
speechtext: Order. May I say that there is no question of privilege here. If the hon. member wishes to make a speech on the topic of the abolition or retention of the death penalty, he will be able to do so in due course.

Mr. Speaker, very soon the Canadian people through their representatives in this house, will in conscience vote upon whether to retain capital punishment in this country. This is a serious matter to all of us in the house. The motion before us is a serious matter to hon. members and Canadians generally. Some of us thought there would be introduced a resolution which we could consider and perhaps amend until it was more generally acceptable not only to this house but to the Canadian people at large.
Criminal Code
It has been mentioned that there will be a free vote on this motion. I appreciate this very much and the people of Canada appreciate having, through their representatives in the house, a free vote on this most important question. We have a very serious responsibility in considering this matter. I mentioned earlier that some of us in this house and many Canadians generally had hoped there would be some qualifications in the motion with regard to the imposition of the death penalty. Many Canadians and hon. members of this house believe that one qualification might be that a person who has escaped from a penitentiary and killed a guard in the process of escaping should be subject to the death penalty. Many people believe that capital punishment should be meted out to a prisoner who commits such a crime.
[DOT] (9:40 p.m.)
There are those, Mr. Speaker, who feel that someone who kills a policeman, a man who is hired to protect society, certainly should receive the death penalty. We are charged with protecting society, too, Mr. Speaker. We have listened to many arguments this afternoon and yesterday, and we will probably listen to many more before this debate is concluded. How far do we go, how deeply do we consider this duty of ours to protect society? As I mentioned a moment ago, there are those who feel that a person who kills a policeman, a man who is hired to protect society, should be meted out the death penalty for that crime.
After listening to the debate, I find there are Canadians who feel there are even worse crimes than murder. I refer to the dope pedlar, for instance, who pushes dope to high school children in Canada. Many people feel that this is an even more heinous crime than murder, because it leads to all sorts of things up and down the scale.
As a representative, Mr. Speaker, I feel that I know what my constituents think. From what I have read, I feel that I know what the Churches of Canada think. I feel I know how the chiefs of police think. I feel I know how I think, personally. As a representative, then, I know full well how I should vote. The question is a simple one when looked at in that way. However, when the time to vote comes closer, and it is rapidly approaching, and I have to stand in my place and, in conscience, as a representative cast my vote upon whether or not we shall retain capital punishment, the problem becomes more serious. It becomes

March 24, 1966
Criminal Code
more serious moment by moment, day by day. A month or two ago I did not think too much about it. A year or so ago, I thought very little about it. Tonight I am thinking of it very seriously, and tomorrow I will think of it more seriously. As I said earlier the Canadian people, in conscience through their representatives in this house, shortly will cast their votes upon whether or not to abolish capital punishment.
I have mentioned conscience, and when I think of conscience I think also of the student of theology. Many of these people, young and old, bring forth the argument-not necessarily the argument, but put forth the idea-as to whether there is a difference between body and soul? I am sure that we, as Christians, must consider this question seriously. Is there a difference between the physical reality and the spiritual reality? Is there then a difference between the natural law and the spiritual law? Is there a difference between natural justice and eternal justice? As I said earlier, we are confronted with these thoughts. We go to a funeral and we are told: This is a piece of clay; the spirit has departed. This is just one of the ideas that we must consider, Mr. Speaker.
The one real argument that is put forward again and again by the abolitionists is that we must grow up; we must become more civilized, that we must treat people differently. I realize it is only about 150 years ago that the death penalty was meted out for people who stole the sum of five shillings or over. It was at this time the idea of abolishing the death penalty was first put forward. Surely, Mr. Speaker, I can agree with that: No one should be put to death for stealing five or ten shillings. Now we have come to the point where we are told we must grow up and we must abolish the death penalty for the ultimate crime. In my opinion, in considering this resolution, I am not too sure we shoud grow up so quickly. We have been told of many countries in which the death penalty has been abolished. We have heard a great deal about the United Kingdom and the United States. Capital punishment has been abolished in England, but I am not too sure the experience has been a happy one. The United States has not seen fit to completely abolish the death penalty. I wonder, Mr. Speaker, if Canada is not trying to grow up too quickly. Perhaps we should go part way; perhaps there should be a qualification and the death penalty should be retained for certain crimes but not for others.

Now, Mr. Speaker, I do not intend to take up very much of the time of this house. I have no intention of going through all the arguments for and against abolition of capital punishment. However, I want the Canadian people to remember that if this motion is carried and capital punishment is abolished, then we will have some other problems. Where do we go from there? For instance, the hon. member who spoke before me mentioned the innocent victims, the members of the family of the person who is charged. I say, Mr. Speaker, we have to consider also not just the one family but we have to consider two families: We have to consider the innocent victims on both sides.
[DOT] (9:50 p.m.)
We have spent very little time considering the innocent victims or their families, and I feel that this consideration should come within the qualifications I mentioned earlier. If we are considering so deeply the person who has committed the crime, we must also give that kind of consideration to the innocent victims on both sides. People in the world today are actually starving to death, yet the parliament of this great country is here considering only a few individuals.
In conclusion, I will mention one other matter. If the death penalty is abolished, then I would ask, Mr. Speaker, whether we should not also consider something else. We are strongly charged with the protection of society, which is the reason I rose in my place this evening. The question is how strong that charge is and how far we can go to protect society. Should we go a step further?
We are all familiar with intelligence tests. All our children submit to them. I am not too sure what they are worth, but they are accepted by society in general as worth while. Therefore I would leave this thought with the house. Should we go a step further and have the psychologist, the doctor, the lawyer, the clergyman and the teacher get together with the scientist and construct a machine which would test each and every one of us early in life, and from time to time through life? Then if certain traits manifest themselves, should we not begin control before the fact?
This is only a thought; I do not advocate this step. I agree with hon. members that a penalty is a deterrent. I do not agree that the death penalty is not a deterrent, and for this reason. Whether we collect a parking ticket, a speeding ticket, or commit any crime, if there
March 24, 1966



was no deterrent our whole correctional system or the protection of our society would collapse and chaos would reign. Therefore I cannot agree that the death penalty is not a deterrent.
I grant you, Mr. Speaker, it is an extreme penalty, but if we do abolish it I think we are bound to consider an alternative. We are still strongly charged with the protection of society, and we cannot fulfil that charge by doing away with deterrents and laws. As I said earlier, we have a penalty for every crime, even a parking ticket. I have heard no amendment moved to this resolution, Mr. Speaker, but I would strongly urge the house, through you, that some qualifications be made in it which would make it more acceptable to this house.

Mr. Speaker, I should like at the outset of my remarks to point up what I think was an inaccuracy in the remarks of the preceding speaker. He made some reference to the need for laws, and the impression I got from his remarks-and the impression I have received from many who appeared to be retentionists -was that there is only one deterrent, if in fact there is any, and that is capital punishment.
It is therefore suggested that the issue is whether we are going to have deterrents or whether our whole legal system is going to break down. I know other speakers have dealt with this point, and the hon. gentleman who just preceded me seemed to be talking along the same lines. I would point out, as others have, that it is erroneous to assume that capital punishment is the only deterrent.
The issue-and this will be the main body of my remarks-has to do with the necessity for capital punishment. I am not one who feels that this is necessarily a moral issue. I suggest, Mr. Speaker, that the morality of killing, of taking human life, is determined by the circumstances. The taking of human life is the highest form of barbarism and is degrading to society. It is degrading whether or not this taking of human life is done by hanging, in war, or even in the case of self-defence. But no one commits an immoral act if he legitimately kills another in an act of self-defence.
Therefore I suggest, if we are all agreed, as my colleague from St. John's East (Mr. O'Keefe) is agreed, that it is a dreadful thing to take human life, and if we agree with the remarks of the hon. member for Prince (Mr. MacDonald), then the issue which must
Criminal Code
be decided in the matter now before the house is the necessity for taking human life.
I suggest that this very important matter ought not to be decided by emotion, by sentiment or suspicion, but by fairness and reason. I suggest that reason is the greatest mark of a civilized society. Therefore, Mr. Speaker, the onus of proving the necessity for maintaining capital punishment is clearly upon the retentionists. They must give the clearest evidence of an imperative need and, I suggest, show beyond reasonable doubt the necessity for the cause which they espouse. We must examine the subject and find grounds to determine the imperative need for convincing evidence which will justify the taking of human life.
The answer, Mr. Speaker, I suggest falls under two headings. The first is retribution.
Ten o'clock.
This is the community's way of expressing its abhorrence of a grievous crime.
Ten o'clock.
Mr. Speaker, hon. members are calling ten o'clock and I am wondering whether it is ten o'clock.

speakerposition: Deputy Whip of the Liberal Party; Chief Government Whip's assistant; Deputy Chair of Committees of the Whole
speechtext:
Has the
hon. member unanimous consent of the house to continue his speech, in view of the time limit he himself mentions?

Agreed.
[DOT] (10:00 p.m.)

As I was saying, retribution is one of the two grounds on which we can find the evidence necessary for establishing whether or not we ought to take human life. The first ground of retribution is the community's way of expressing its abhorrence of the crime of murder, through the gravity of punishment which society extracts. In this way society hopes to impress upon its members the gravity of the crime itself. This is a paradox, I suggest, Mr. Speaker, because the

March 24. 1966
Criminal Code
community is expressing its exereme revulsion at such a crime, and in itself uses the very same means to convey this revulsion. On the long term basis the well-being of the community will be more affected if it does not resort to this type of retribution.
When we speak of deterrent we should look at the facts in order to determine the position we are taking. We must not do this by emotion, or by sentiment, or by fear. It has long been said that it is the abolitionists who are the sentimentalists. I believe that an earlier speaker has already quoted Sir Ernest Gower's book "A life for a life". Sir Ernest confessed that when he began the study of this matter he was convinced-and this seems to be the widespread feeling among those with whom I have discussed the matter-that sentiment was on the side of the abolitionists and reason on the side of the retentionists. At the end of the four years which it took to complete this work, he had to reverse himself. He came to the conclusion that reason was on the side of the abolitionists and sentiment on the side of the retentionists.
We must ask ourselves, Mr. Speaker, what are the facts? What is the evidence? What evidence can be put forth by the retentionists, who suggest that the death penalty is such a unique deterrent as to warrant its retention by society?
There are, I would suggest, in general three kinds of killers. There is the psychopath or the sex offender. People of that type are not subject to normal restraints. For these men perhaps there is no such thing as a deterrent. They are sick. Unless we publicly support a policy whereby we say to these sick people: "We cannot cope with you in society; therefore if this illness becomes evident, we will extract you out of society," then I suggest there is no reason for capital punishment; because many people of that ilk might commit crimes which may not result in the taking of human life, but which could be very serious in society. Those people can be equally a menace to society whether or not they have a particular tendency to the taking of human life, or something just short of that.
Really, if we are going to kill them because they are not the normal kinds of people in society, we should perhaps kill them before they take a human life, if they show any tendency in that direction. I would suggest that this is the logic that must be employed by anybody who would kill them, if in fact they were guilty of murder.

Of course there are those people you might term the one-shot offenders, who commit murder in anger, or under the influence of alcohol, or under a particular set of circumstances. These are the once-in-a-lifetime murderers. These people are obviously not going to be deterred by capital punishment, and perhaps they will not be deterred by anything else.
We then come to the group which is causing most concern, perhaps, the group of the professional killer. The evidence, as other hon. members have mentioned, suggests that for these people there is no difference between this kind of deterrent and any other kind of deterrent. If you will, they are equally effective or equally ineffective.
There are in this house probably a great number of hon. members who fought in the war. I was not among them because I was not one of the nine-year olds who was conscripted. I am sure that you may recall this suggestion which was made by a man who had spent some time in the war. He said that if you were asked to do something dangerous you did not say to yourself, "I will not do that because I will be killed, but I will do it because I will only lose a limb or I will only lose an eye."
The thinking process, if any, as I understand it from those who have discussed this with me was, "I will do it because I think I will get away with it", and most people who think they can get away with it, do it. Those who withdrew were people who did not think they could get away with it.
I have a great deal of respect for my colleague from St. John's East (Mr. O'Keefe), and I disagreed with what I thought was a rather unkind and unwarranted gesture on the part of the hon. member for Kootenay West (Mr. Herridge), when he rose on his facetious question of privilege. But I would like to say to my colleague from St. John's East, with whom I disagree on this point, that I can well understand and respect his position, but I think he is like a great many other Canadians in looking at this matter and saying, "I would be deterred from doing it, therefore others will also." But these, Mr. Speaker, are precisely the people who would not be doing it anyway.
When we are talking about this as a deterrent we ought to realize that the greatest deterrent is detection. There are certain communities in Canada that have a high incidence of traffic infractions. I can give an example of neighbouring municipalities. In
March 24, 1966

Criminal Code
one municipality fines for traffic infractions are higher than in the other, but it is notorious that motorists speed in that municipality. However, they do not speed in the other municipality because the police there are more on the ball and they know they will be detected. So if it is a deterrent perhaps only the professionals, however many they may be, are the ones who would really consider this is a deterrent; but the best deterrent obviously is detection.
I should now like to give a quotation. Although I have tried to listen to most of the debate, I do not know if this quotation has been given already. When I read it I suggest many hon. members will not know whether the quotation is from a present-day retention-ist or a man who actually made the statement 150 years ago. It is:
Repeal this law and see the contrast. No man can trust himself for an hour out of doors without the most alarming apprehensions that on his return every vestige of his property will be swept off by the hardened robber.
No, Mr. Speaker, he was not talking about capital punishment as it applied to the murder of a prison guard. These were the words of Lord Ellenborough, when he abhored a change in the law that permitted a person charged with stealing five shillings to be hanged.
While I respect the sincerity of all those who are retentionists I suggest that any study of the debates on this matter over the past 150 years does not show the position has changed one bit since the time of Lord Ellenborough, and the evidence of every study undertaken continues to prove that Lord Ellenborough was wrong. And, as Lord Ellenborough was wrong in 1810, I suggest that those who take the same position today will perhaps in a decade, I hope, or 25 years, look back on some of the things that were said in this debate and regard them in the same light as they regard what Lord Ellenborough said in relation to the offence of stealing five shillings.
Would the hon. member care to explain the position taken by nine attorneys general in Canada today?

I am glad my colleague asked that question. I may suggest by the answer I am going to give him that I asked him to ask it, but I did not. I cannot suppose what the attorneys general think; but I know a very distinguished ex-attorney general from the other side of the house spoke on this matter, and he is the only attorney general, other
than the one in my own province, with whom I discussed the matter.
I would say that perhaps one of the fears of the attorneys general is that this could have a demoralizing effect on policemen and prison guards. I have met individuals who otherwise accept my reasoning but say it is a very serious matter for prison guards and the policemen. We must respect their views, but the reason they would exempt the murder of prison guards and policemen from the abolition of capital punishment is not so much for the deterrent effect but because its retention is important for the morale of the police and prison guard force.
[DOT] (10:10 p.m.)
Now, perhaps if that much were so and if perhaps in the next year or two our police force were to disintegrate, then perhaps we might be justified in saying because it is a deterrent in respect of police officers we will be justified in taking a human life in order to be able to have a police force. In that case I think we would be obliged to do that. However, I am quite sure that would not be the case. There are now 13 states in the United States which are abolitionist states. Looking at the records there and looking at the facts, I suggest to my hon. colleague from St. John's East and the attorney general from Newfoundland who is of the same view as the hon. member for St. John's East (Mr. O'Keefe)-
May I ask a question, Mr. Speaker? I would like to ask the hon. member whether he knows of any case where a person was convicted of murder who did not have the benefit of psychiatric examination?

Mr. Speaker, I regret that unlike many other members of this house I have not had a distinguished career before the bar. My experience is purely academic; but from the study I have made I was abhorred by what we regard as insanity and by the many cases where the exact conditions you outlined did not exist. Recently I read a book entitled "In Cold Blood". This was the most vicious crime one could imagine. Four persons in a family were killed. I do not know what reaction others might have but I do know of one person very close to me who has had perhaps a different view of it than I had from reading that book. I think the result was that it made her less convinced of her view of retention and made me stronger in my own view of abolition. If you read about that case, the boy who actually killed that

Business of the House
man did not think as he killed him; he thought what a nice man he was. He was not killing that man; he was killing his father. I do not think we are enhanced by killing him, unless we say we do not want that man in society, and then we should take him out; but that man should have been taken out long ago.
We should be finding out who these people are at an early stage in life and should be getting rid of them. Nothing was served by killing that man. To say to the contrary is to fly in the face of reason, to fly in the face of the views of the criminologists and sociologists who have made a study of this matter. I say it is important not to approach this by emotion or sentiment. If we are to adopt a position, let us know what it is. If we are to continue on with capital punishment, let us know why we are doing it. Are we doing it for vengeance or because we do think this has some kind of deterrent effect and one which is greater or more unique than any other? If the latter is our view, let us prove it.
I am grateful to the house for the time they have given me this evening. I would hope that the consensus now would be one of fact over sentiment, of reason over emotion, and of hope over fear.

Mr. Speaker, the matter I wish to raise tonight with the Minister of Labour or his parliamentary secretary, who is here, arises out of a statement attributed to the president of the National Homebuilders Association speaking in Montreal, in which he stated that in his view a growing shortage of mortgage money is creating the danger of a critical stoppage in construction in this important industry. He has suggested that the government should re-enter the field of direct mortgage loans for speculative housing.
It is becoming apparent that there is a general tightening of the money supply in Canada at the present time, which has two effects. One, interest rates on mortgages rise because of competition for available money and, two, such investment funds as are available tend to shift out of the N.H.A. field, because of its controlled interest rate, and to move to more lucrative fields, conventional mortgages and industrial and commercial properties.
As conventional lenders shift to non-N.H.A. loan areas, the market dries up and the construction industry tends to slow down. To date this may not appear as a serious problem, but the clouds are on the horizon. Because of the importance of the building industry to have some indication of government policy, I hope that the government, if it cannot do so tonight, will consider making some type of extended statement in this regard.
Those of us who are associated with clients in the construction industry realize that builders must plan a long time in advance. If there is any danger of a mortgage shortage accumulating during the year, unless they know whether or not the government is prepared to act, it is virtually impossible to design a housebuilding program for the entire year. No matter what the government's answer is, I hope at some early stage it will make a decision and an announcement. Does the government intend to re-enter the direct
March 24. 1966

lending field if a mortgage shortage develops and, if so, to what extent? I hope it will tell the building industry either yes or no. It does not really matter which it is, as long as a decision is made so that other decisions can be based upon it.
Does the government intend to permit banks to enter the N.H.A. field to supply some of the needed funds? Is the government giving any thought to trying to design some orderly consistent method of providing mortgage financing in Canada? Up to now it has been turned on and off like a tap, largely for economic reasons, and the building industry has never felt that there was any reliable and constant source of mortgage money on which it could base its plans.
[DOT] (10:20 p.m.)
Finally, when and where does the government intend to honour its election pledge that N.H.A. financing will be extended to older homes? All the Liberal literature circulated in the urban areas in the last two election campaigns carried this promise, and we have so far seen no signs of its being fulfilled. I hope that the government will consider making a statement as to its intentions so that the people interested in this matter may know what the program is to be.
As I said, Mr. Speaker, this could become a serious problem. The building industry must know a year or more in advance where it is going. Builders cannot buy land, service it and make all the necessary commitments unless they are assured that there will be an orderly supply of mortgage financing available. Even though the building industry is continuing at a very good rate, all the signs at the present time indicate that there is a continuing shortage of mortgage financing. Because of the importance to the industry, because of the need to make decisions now for the balance of the year, I hope that if he cannot do so in the three minutes available now, the parliamentary secretary will urge the minister to make a full statement at an early date.

I shall bring to the attention of the minister the many thought-provoking questions the hon. member has raised. In the meantime I should like at least to place on

The suggestion, for instance, that the housing industry is to be jeopardized by a shortage of money is a problematical one. It might be of interest to hon. members to know that at the end of 1965 there were 120,000 housing units under construction in Canada. Because of this very high carry-over and the further fact that the whole housing construction industry is working to full capacity at the present time, it is expected that during 1966 not only will this level be maintained but the indications are that, despite the fears of representatives of the housing industry and despite the fears voiced tonight by the hon. member for Danforth, housing construction will surpass the record year of 1965.
The hon. member has made a point about planning in advance. He mentioned that this should be done a long time ahead. I am not too sure whether by "a long time ahead" he means three months, six months or a year. But I am sure that when the minister returns and has an opportunity to voice his opinion on future policy in this connection, he will cover this question. In the meantime, Mr. Speaker, I should like to make this point to the hon. member. National Housing Act mortgage lending the approved lenders and by C.M.H.C. was 33 per cent higher during the first two months of 1966 as compared to 1965, and housing starts were six per cent higher during the first two months of this year as compared to 1965. This is hardly a very gloomy picture.
Furthermore, during the past three years C.M.H.C. has been authorized to make speculative building loans in support of the winter housing incentive program, and approximately 22,000 such loans were made during the last four months of 1965. maintopic: HARBOURS-VANCOUVER-INQUIRY AS TO PROPOSED WHARF DEVELOPMENT
HARBOURS-VANCOUVER-INQUIRY AS TO PROPOSED WHARF DEVELOPMENT
speechtext:
A couple of weeks ago the Minister of Transport (Mr. Pickersgill) came out to the west coast to visit the harbour of Vancouver, to have a look at its facilities and to learn a little more about the great debate, some of the furore which was surrounding this harbour. He looked at that time at the C.P.R. property which forms one of the major elements of the Vancouver harbour. The C.P.R. property in Vancouver harbour is in a state of neglect. I do not need to enlarge too much upon this. It has been debated in the house, in committee and this story has appeared in the press many times.
The Canadian Pacific occupies piers that are condemned, old wharves that are no longer suitable for modern shipping. At the foot of Granville Street, the main street of Vancouver, it has a burnt out old pier which is marked on marine maps as a ruin. We want to see this end of the harbour, the best available deep waterlots in Canada today, properly developed. This is what we wanted the minister to see. We would like the minister to tell us what the National Harbours Board and the government of Canada are going to do in Vancouver this year.
The property in question has long been under dispute between the government of Canada and the Canadian Pacific. Historically the dispute goes back to 1884, when the steel came in as far as Port Moody and stopped there. This was the obligation of the Canadian Pacific to bring the steel through to Tidewater, which is at Port Moody. Then the company decided to move into the city of Vancouver, and when they moved into the city of Vancouver they assumed that they were given further grants along the right-of-way. The question of whether these grants were to be interpreted in the same way as the original land grants along the right-of-way up to Port Moody is the question under dispute.
There are areas in Vancouver harbour which have been under legal dispute since 1930 and the revenue from this property is put into escrow. What we would like to know
[The Acting Speaker (Mr. Rinfret).]
is this: When are the government and the Canadian Pacific going to get together and settle this long, historic dispute so that Vancouver can enjoy the development of these lands. We have to await the end of this dispute before proper wharves and piers can be built to serve this Canadian western port. We want to know whether or not there is to be expropriation of Canadian Pacific property, whether the Canadian Pacific itself can be encouraged to develop the property. There are rumours and stories in the Vancouver newspapers today that $50 million is to be spent by the National Harbours Board in this area. We know the dispute has not yet been settled. The minister has hinted at some things but we want something more definitive. I hope the parliamentary secretary will be able to say something about it tonight.

It seems almost presumptuous of me to imply that I know more about Vancouver harbour than he does. I am sure I can add little to what he already knows. However, there are plans for the development of wharves on the south shore of the Vancouver side of the harbour for general cargo facilities which will require the use of the property now under dispute with the Canadian Pacific Railway. It is hoped that this property dispute can be settled quickly so that the early orderly development of harbour facilities can take place.
I understand that the minister was in Vancouver earlier this month. He did say that he hoped and expected that this dispute would be settled at a relatively early date, certainly within this year.

LABOUR CONDITIONS-ATLANTIC REGION-STEPS TO IMPROVE UNEMPLOYMENT SITUATION
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, the Minister of Finance can accept the fact that the content of my question, which we are now debating, will be the basis of numerous questions and speeches unless he takes special steps open to him to guarantee a continuing climate for expansion in the Atlantic area. We have the double-barrelled problem of keeping pace with the expansion in the remainder of Canada and of gaining
March 24, 1966	COMMONS
back the ground lost through a lack of interest and attention until the Diefenbaker administration took office in 1957. We recall very well the damage to our economic progress during the last period that a Liberal administration put into effect a national tight money policy that retarded our advancement, and members on this side of the house will not sit idly by and watch this happen again.
The national rate of unemployment in this nation as of February 19, according to the Dominion Bureau of Statistics figures, stood at 5 per cent, with more than 350,000 individuals unemployed. This is not a figure to brag about, for it indicates the extent of human suffering in our nation today. The shocking aspect of these figures is that 65,000 of these individuals and almost 11 per cent of the working population of the Atlantic provinces is included in this group. Over-expansion, boom and prosperity are foreign words in the Atlantic provinces, and tight money will only guarantee less hope of their ever being removed from the vocabulary of our people.
A new philosophy has been nurtured in the Atlantic provinces since the days of the Diefenbaker administration which produced programs and policies that were geared to find solutions to the special problems of our area. These programs were of significant benefit to the provincial governments in carrying forward their programs of development.
Since the present administration has taken office we have found little of the philosophy that was so evident between 1957 and 1963. With the one exception of an increase in assistance in the construction of the trans-Canada highway, we have witnessed a disinterest in our special problems. The Atlantic Development Board, while helpful within the confines of the amended legislation, does not have the financial resources available to it that will make the impact on our economy we had anticipated when we established it. We have not enjoyed the same degree of favour from this administration, and with the fractured thinking within the cabinet there is little hope in the foreseeable future for expecting the kind of approach we must have if we are to progress at the rate we consider advisable for the nation's good.
The minister has available to him the means of alleviating the tight money policy in so far as the Atlantic provinces are concerned. There

He can take the first step next Tuesday evening, when he brings down his budget, by recognizing the recommendations of the second annual review of the Economic Council of Canada, which appears on pages 175 and 176 of that report. We have a right to expect this kind of approach from the Minister of Finance, and he may rest assured that his inaction in this regard will lead to a concentrated and continuing attack from members in the Progressive Conservative party until such action is forthcoming.

subtopic: LETTER FROM QUEBEC PREMIER RESPECTING CONSTITUTION AMENDMENT

speechtext:
February 17th, 1966.
The Honourable Lester B. Pearson,
Prime Minister,
Government of Canada,
Ottawa, Ont.
My dear Prime Minister:
Your reply of January 26th to my letter of January 20th has been brought to the attention of my Cabinet colleagues who have thoroughly examined its contents.
After full consideration, and for the reasons set out in my letter, the Government of Quebec feels that it must maintain its decision to postpone indefinitely the study of the present proposed amendment to the constitution.
Of course, if such is the desire of the Government of Canada or of the other provinces, Quebec has no intention to oppose the
reconsidering, at a future federal-provincial conference, of the repatriation of the constitution in the light of the circumstances mentioned in our letters.
In any event, I must add that we are most anxious to see the Quebec Parliament Act adopted. If this question is not settled as envisaged it will have to be taken up again in any discussion of a new formula for the repatriation of the constitution.
I readily understand your disappointment at the decision taken by the Government of Quebec. You may rest assured, however, that in this matter my colleagues and I have never questioned the basic aim that our constitution should become absolutely and truly our own.
With my best regards,
Sincerely yours,
Jean Lesage.
Friday, March 25, 1966
